c10_bio_ch01.title: Use it in the wild
c10_bio_ch01.scenario: At kilometre 30 of a marathon, a runner 'hits the wall': pace collapses, legs feel heavy, and his blood shows high lactate with depleted glucose. His friend shouts to just breathe harder and push through.
c10_bio_ch01.prompt: What actually explains the crash — and what helps?

options.text: His muscle glycogen is exhausted, so cells lean on anaerobic glycolysis; lactate and H+ build up, inhibiting the enzymes and contraction. Easing pace and taking carbs helps — faster breathing can't instantly raise oxygen delivery or clear lactate.
options.outcome: Recovery takes time: lactate must be oxidised in the muscle or shipped to the liver, and oxygen supply is limited by cardiac output, not just how fast he breathes.

options.text: The muscles ran out of oxygen, so breathing as fast as possible will immediately convert the lactate back into energy.
options.outcome: Oxygen delivery is capped by cardiac output and capillary diffusion; lactate still has to be cleared biochemically, which takes minutes, not a breath.

options.text: It's simple dehydration — a glass of water and he can sprint again.
options.outcome: Water helps hydration but doesn't restore glycogen or remove the acidosis blocking contraction.

c10_bio_ch02.title: Use it in the wild
c10_bio_ch02.scenario: A wheat farmer's field is overrun with broadleaf weeds. The agri-store sells 2,4-D, a synthetic auxin. Wheat is a monocot; the weeds are dicots.
c10_bio_ch02.prompt: Will spraying 2,4-D clear the weeds without hurting the wheat?

options.text: Yes — 2,4-D mimics auxin, and dicots are far more sensitive to it: the overdose triggers uncontrolled, lethal growth in the weeds while the wheat tolerates or breaks it down.
options.outcome: Selective herbicide action: the same hormone-mimic exploits the difference in sensitivity between dicots and monocots.

options.text: No — any plant hormone will boost all plants equally, so it will just feed the weeds.
options.outcome: Sensitivity differs hugely by plant group; dicots are killed by auxin overload at doses monocots shrug off.

options.text: Use cytokinin instead — encouraging cell division will make the wheat outgrow the weeds.
options.outcome: Cytokinin doesn't kill weeds; competition alone won't clear an established weed infestation.

c10_bio_ch03.title: Use it in the wild
c10_bio_ch03.scenario: In a seed lab, a trainee sorts seeds by the rule 'monocots keep endosperm, dicots never have it.' A castor seed — a dicot full of endosperm — lands on her bench and doesn't fit the rule.

options.text: By whether the endosperm survives into the mature seed, not by monocot vs dicot: castor keeps its endosperm (albuminous), while pea and bean absorb theirs into the cotyledons.
options.outcome: Both monocots and dicots come in albuminous and exalbuminous types — it's about seed development, not taxonomy.

options.text: Castor must be mislabelled — all dicots absorb their endosperm.
options.outcome: Castor and coconut are textbook dicots/monocots with persistent endosperm; the mature seed tells the truth, not the group name.

options.text: Cut the seed open; whichever side has more starch is a monocot.
options.outcome: Endosperm persistence is a developmental trait — the scutellum in maize or castor's endosperm don't change the plant's class.

c10_bio_ch04.title: Use it in the wild
c10_bio_ch04.scenario: Birds keep eating the brightest fish in a pond. A classmate concludes: 'The fish will evolve duller colours because they need to hide from the birds.'
c10_bio_ch04.prompt: What's the right way to explain what will actually happen?

options.text: Colour variation already exists at random; birds simply eat bright fish more often, so dull fish survive and breed more — dull colour spreads over generations.
options.outcome: Natural selection works on existing heritable variation; the population changes because of who survives, not because anyone 'needs' to change.

options.text: She's right — facing predators pushes fish to produce duller offspring on purpose.
options.outcome: Mutations aren't aimed at a goal; predation only selects among variants that already exist.

options.text: Each bright fish will gradually darken its own scales to match the pond bottom.
options.outcome: An acquired colour change isn't written into the genes, so it wouldn't shift the population's colours over generations.

c10_chem_ch01.title: Use it in the wild
c10_chem_ch01.scenario: In a metal-extraction demo, coke reduces iron oxide: 2Fe2O3 + 3C → 4Fe + 3CO2. A junior technician logs 'carbon is reduced, since it gains oxygen to become CO2.'

options.text: No — carbon gains oxygen and loses electrons, so it is oxidised and acts as the reducing agent; Fe2O3 loses oxygen and is reduced, making it the oxidising agent.
options.outcome: Gaining oxygen is oxidation by the classical definition, and electron loss confirms it — the carbon does the reducing.

options.text: Yes — 'gains oxygen' sounds like a gain, and gain means reduction.
options.outcome: Reduction is gain of electrons (or loss of oxygen); gaining oxygen is the opposite — oxidation.

options.text: Both are right — carbon is oxidised and reduced at the same time.
options.outcome: A species can't be both here; C goes to CO2 (oxidation) while Fe3+ goes to Fe (reduction).

c10_chem_ch02.title: Use it in the wild
c10_chem_ch02.scenario: A quality-control lab receives an unlabelled white powder. It dissolves cleanly in dilute hydrochloric acid with no gas, and it also reacts with hot sodium hydroxide solution.
c10_chem_ch02.prompt: What kind of substance is it?

options.text: An amphoteric oxide such as zinc oxide — it behaves as a base toward the acid and as an acid toward the alkali because it sits between metallic and non-metallic character.
options.outcome: Amphoteric oxides like ZnO and Al2O3 neutralise both HCl and NaOH, e.g. ZnO + 2HCl → ZnCl2 + H2O and ZnO + 2NaOH → Na2ZnO2 + H2O.

options.text: A neutral salt — it dissolves in both, so it must be inert to both.
options.outcome: It isn't merely dissolving; it chemically neutralises each — a neutral salt wouldn't react with NaOH at all.

options.text: A strong base, because anything that reacts with acid is a base.
options.outcome: The reaction with NaOH rules that out — strong bases don't also neutralise bases.

c10_chem_ch03.title: Use it in the wild
c10_chem_ch03.scenario: A recycler wants to cut costs on an aluminium plant. He proposes skipping the expensive electrolysis and just heating alumina (Al2O3) with coke, the way iron is won from haematite in a blast furnace.
c10_chem_ch03.prompt: Will the coke trick work for aluminium?

options.text: No — aluminium sits above carbon in the reactivity series, so carbon can't pull oxygen away from Al2O3; only electrolysis supplies enough energy to reduce it.
options.outcome: Carbon reduces only the oxides of metals below it — that works for iron but fails for aluminium, which is why Hall-Heroult electrolysis exists.

options.text: Yes — a hotter furnace and more coke can reduce any oxide.
options.outcome: Temperature isn't the deciding factor; the reactivity series is. Carbon simply can't displace a metal more reactive than itself.

options.text: Yes — iron and aluminium are extracted identically in industry anyway.
options.outcome: They aren't: iron uses carbon reduction in a blast furnace, aluminium uses electrolysis precisely because carbon can't do the job.

c10_chem_ch04.title: Use it in the wild
c10_chem_ch04.scenario: Three unlabelled hydrocarbon fuels arrive at a lab. A technician adds orange bromine water to each: samples B and C turn colourless, sample A stays orange.
c10_chem_ch04.prompt: What has she learned about sample A?

options.text: A is a saturated hydrocarbon — an alkane with only single bonds, so there is no double or triple bond for bromine to add across; B and C are unsaturated.
options.outcome: Decolourising bromine water is the classic test for C=C or C≡C bonds; alkanes only substitute (slowly, in light) and leave the colour intact.

options.text: A failed the test, so it isn't a hydrocarbon at all.
options.outcome: Alkanes are hydrocarbons too — they just lack the pi bonds that decolourise bromine.

options.text: A is the most reactive — it didn't waste time reacting with bromine.
options.outcome: No colour change means no addition happened; unsaturation, not inertness, is what reacts fast with bromine.

c10_chem_ch05.title: Use it in the wild
c10_chem_ch05.scenario: Reading the periodic table, a student predicts calcium (Group 2, Period 4) will react more gently with water than magnesium (Group 2, Period 3): 'It's heavier, so its electrons are held tighter.'

options.text: No — ionisation energy falls down the group because extra shells shield the outer electrons, so calcium lets go of them more easily and reacts more vigorously with water.
options.outcome: Ca + 2H2O → Ca(OH)2 + H2 is livelier than magnesium's slow reaction — reactivity rises down Group 2.

options.text: Yes — higher atomic number always means stronger hold on electrons.
options.outcome: Atomic number rises, but so do shells and shielding; down a group the outer electrons are actually lost more easily.

options.text: Neither — all Group 2 metals react with water at the same rate.
options.outcome: The trend is real and visible: Mg barely reacts with cold water while Ca bubbles steadily.

c10_eco_ch01.title: Use it in the wild
c10_eco_ch01.scenario: A newspaper reports that State X has higher per-capita income than State Y, yet a larger share of underweight children. A columnist concludes: 'Income growth does nothing for nutrition.'
c10_eco_ch01.prompt: What's the strongest reading of the data?

options.text: Income is only an average — if growth is unequally shared or sanitation is poor, children stay underweight despite rising income; check long-term indicators like stunting rates before judging.
options.outcome: Development is multi-dimensional: health outcomes depend on distribution, public services and absorption of nutrients, not the average wallet.

options.text: The data must be wrong — higher income always means better-nourished children.
options.outcome: Per-capita income can rise while poor households and sanitation lag; the paradox is real, not a data error.

options.text: Income is meaningless — only calorie counts matter for development.
options.outcome: Income still matters; the point is it doesn't capture health, education or equity on its own.

c10_eco_ch02.title: Use it in the wild
c10_eco_ch02.scenario: A district report shows MGNREGA households averaged about 50 days of work against the 100-day guarantee, women did over half the person-days, and states still owe thousands of crores in pending wages. An official says the shortfall proves villagers don't want the work.
c10_eco_ch02.prompt: How should the 50-day figure be read?

options.text: Households mainly need fallback work in the lean season — roughly 50-60 days — and rising non-farm wages pull some away; the real failure to chase is the wage backlog, which violates the 15-day payment rule.
options.outcome: Low average take-up reflects when the work is needed, not the scheme's worth; unpaid wages are the actionable violation.

options.text: Fifty days means the guarantee is pointless and the scheme should be scrapped.
options.outcome: A guarantee is a safety net — people use what they need; lean-season demand explains the average without making it useless.

options.text: It proves households prefer leisure to guaranteed wages.
options.outcome: The demand is seasonal and wage-delayed; laziness doesn't explain women supplying 54% of the person-days.

c10_eco_ch03.title: Use it in the wild
c10_eco_ch03.scenario: A women's self-help group has built a corpus of several lakh rupees through monthly savings and internal lending at 2% a month. A bank offers them a low-interest loan; the village moneylender offers a bigger sum instantly at 3% a month.
c10_eco_ch03.prompt: Which door should they knock on?

options.text: The bank — the SHG's joint liability and peer pressure work as 'social collateral,' which is exactly what unlocks cheap formal credit for people with no property to pledge.
options.outcome: Repayment discipline is enforced socially, so the bank can lend at rates the moneylender's 3%-a-month compounding can't match.

options.text: The moneylender — more money, faster, no paperwork.
options.outcome: Speed is the trap: monthly rates compound brutally and informal loans carry no consumer protection, which is how debt spirals start.

options.text: Neither — groups that lend to each other should never borrow outside.
options.outcome: Bank linkage is how SHGs scale up; refusing formal credit wastes the social collateral they've already built.

c10_eco_ch04.title: Use it in the wild
c10_eco_ch04.scenario: A small powerloom owner buys yarn at market price and sells grey cloth locally. Since cheap imports surged, his profits have collapsed. A buyer suggests he 'just export directly — globalisation is a free market.'

options.text: Pool with other small units — a cluster or cooperative can share certification, marketing and larger orders, spreading the fixed costs a single small loom can't carry.
options.outcome: Export compliance and small order sizes are scale problems; collective organisation gives small producers the economies of scale a composite mill gets internally.

options.text: Export alone anyway — globalisation means anyone can sell anywhere.
options.outcome: Market access isn't free: quality certification and minimum order sizes are fixed costs that crush a 20-loom unit.

options.text: Lobby for a total ban on imports — that's the only way small producers survive.
options.outcome: Protectionism ignores the real gap — scale and compliance capacity — and closed markets carry their own costs for consumers and competitiveness.

c10_eco_ch05.title: Use it in the wild
c10_eco_ch05.scenario: A shopper pays Rs 450 for a 1-litre bottle of 'virgin coconut oil' bearing an FSSAI licence number and an Agmark logo. At home the oil solidifies at 28°C though pure coconut oil sets near 24°C, and the bottle holds only 880 g against the labelled 910 g.

options.text: Keep the bottle, bill and photos as evidence, get a lab test if needed, and file a complaint — the raised solidification point signals adulteration and the weight gap is under-weighing, regardless of the logos.
options.outcome: A licence number shows registration, not purity; evidence plus the consumer forum is the working remedy.

options.text: Nothing — an FSSAI licence and Agmark on the label guarantee the oil is pure.
options.outcome: Logos can be printed or faked; the physical evidence (solidification point, short weight) overrides the label.

options.text: Just leave a bad review online — reviews are the modern consumer court.
options.outcome: A review warns others but recovers nothing; adulteration and short weight are legal violations the forum can actually redress.

c10_math_ch01.title: Use it in the wild
c10_math_ch01.scenario: Marking a friend's proof that root-3 is irrational, you read: 'a squared equals 3b squared, so a is a multiple of 3.' The teacher docked a mark at exactly that line.

options.text: The justification: since 3 is prime and divides a squared, the prime-factor theorem forces 3 to divide a — and the same theorem is needed later for b.
options.outcome: The proof's engine is 'if a prime divides a square, it divides the number'; stating it makes the contradiction airtight.

options.text: Nothing — a square being a multiple of 3 obviously means the number is too.
options.outcome: 'Obviously' is the skipped step; without the prime theorem the argument has a hole a marker must dock.

options.text: She should have started by assuming root-3 is rational — that's the missing line.
options.outcome: She did assume it via 'root-3 = a/b'; the gap is the divisibility theorem, not the setup.

c10_math_ch02.title: Use it in the wild
c10_math_ch02.scenario: A friend coding a polynomial-divider app claims a shortcut: 'If p(x) divided by (x-a)(x-b) leaves remainder R(x), then the remainder on dividing by (x-a) alone is just R(a).'
c10_math_ch02.prompt: Should the app use the shortcut?

options.text: Yes — since p(x) = (x-a)(x-b)Q(x) + R(x), plugging in x = a kills the divisor term, so p(a) = R(a); by the remainder theorem that is the remainder for division by (x-a).
options.outcome: The remainder theorem turns evaluation into remainder-reading — the shortcut is a theorem, not a hack.

options.text: No — every new divisor needs a fresh long division; remainders don't transfer.
options.outcome: They do: evaluating at the root of any factor collapses p to R there, which is exactly what the remainder theorem uses.

options.text: Only if R(x) is a constant — a linear remainder breaks it.
options.outcome: Degree doesn't matter; p(a) = R(a) holds whatever R looks like, because the (x-a) factor still vanishes at x = a.

c10_math_ch03.title: Use it in the wild
c10_math_ch03.scenario: Solving for fruit prices, a student hits 3x + 2y = 12 and 6x + 4y = 24. Cross-multiplication gives x/0 = y/0 = 1/0, and he writes 'x = y = 0, unique solution.'

options.text: The two equations are the same straight line — every point on it is a solution, so there are infinitely many; 0/0 is undefined, not zero.
options.outcome: When all ratios coincide the equations are dependent (coincident lines); the vanishing denominators are the signal of infinite solutions.

options.text: Zero over zero equals zero, so his x = y = 0 stands.
options.outcome: 0/0 is indeterminate — and (0,0) doesn't even satisfy the equations, since 0 + 0 isn't 12.

options.text: A zero denominator proves the equations have no solution at all.
options.outcome: No-solution happens when the sides are proportional but the constants aren't (parallel lines); here constants match too, giving infinitely many solutions.

c10_math_ch04.title: Use it in the wild
c10_math_ch04.scenario: A boat runs at 15 km/h in still water. It goes 30 km upstream and returns in 4.5 hours total. A trainee says 'the stream could be any speed — the equation will sort it out.'
c10_math_ch04.prompt: Does a real stream speed exist?

options.text: Yes — the timings reduce to x squared = 25 with discriminant 100 > 0, giving x = 5 km/h; the negative root is physically meaningless, not a second answer.
options.outcome: A positive discriminant guarantees real roots; the upstream/downstream model then selects the positive one as the actual stream speed.

options.text: Two real roots mean two valid stream speeds: +5 and -5 km/h.
options.outcome: Speed can't be negative; the minus root is an algebraic leftover, not a physical option.

options.text: No — since time is fixed, any equation for the stream must be contradictory.
options.outcome: The equation is perfectly consistent; checking the discriminant before solving shows a real positive speed exists.

c10_math_ch05.title: Use it in the wild
c10_math_ch05.scenario: A savings app shows total savings after n weeks follows S(n) = 3n squared + 5n (in tens of rupees). The product team asks: 'What's the weekly deposit pattern, and what's the week-15 deposit?'
c10_math_ch05.prompt: How do you recover the AP?

options.text: First term a = S(1) = 8, and the common difference is twice the n-squared coefficient, so d = 6; the 15th deposit is a + 14d = 92 (i.e. Rs 920).
options.outcome: For S(n) = An squared + Bn, the underlying AP always has a = A + B and d = 2A — the quadratic coefficient is half the difference.

options.text: The first deposit is 3 — the coefficient of n squared is the starting term.
options.outcome: That coefficient is half the common difference (d = 2A); the first term is S(1) = 3 + 5 = 8.

options.text: Deposit amounts can't be recovered from a total — you'd need the app data.
options.outcome: S(n) encodes everything: S(1) gives a, and a(n) = S(n) - S(n-1) gives every term.

c10_math_ch06.title: Use it in the wild
c10_math_ch06.scenario: An architect's roof truss has sides 6 m and 8 m meeting at 60°. A modelmaker builds a scale version with 15 cm and 20 cm sides, also at 60°, and a checker asks: 'Prove the model is similar — did you measure the third side?'
c10_math_ch06.prompt: Is the similarity proven without the third side?

options.text: Yes — the included angle matches and the flanking sides share one ratio (600/15 = 800/20 = 40), so SAS similarity holds; every length just scales by 40.
options.outcome: SAS similarity needs two proportional sides plus the equal included angle — the third side then follows automatically at the same scale.

options.text: No — similarity requires all three sides measured and compared.
options.outcome: SSS is only one route; SAS and AA each prove similarity without touching the third side.

options.text: No — the units differ (metres vs centimetres), so the triangles can't be similar.
options.outcome: Similarity is about ratios, not units; converting to the same unit is exactly what reveals the common factor of 40.

c10_math_ch07.title: Use it in the wild
c10_math_ch07.scenario: A student argues: "The distance between (2, 3) and (5, 7) is 7 because the horizontal distance is 3 and vertical distance is 4, and 3+4=7." Is the student correct?
c10_math_ch07.prompt: You are asked: "Explain why the distance formula uses squares and square root instead of just adding the horizontal and vertical distances. Draw a diagram to support your explanation" — what do you conclude?

options.text: The student is incorrect. The straight-line distance (hypotenuse) is 5 units, not 7.
options.outcome: The formula uses squares and square root because of the Pythagoras theorem: in a right triangle, the square of the hypotenuse equals the sum of squares of the legs.

options.text: The most frequent exam error is writing the distance as √((x2 - x1)2 + (y2 - y1)2) = (x2 - x1) + (y2 - y1) by incorrectly "distributing" the square root over addition: √(a2 + b2) = a + b.
options.outcome: For example, for points (0,0) and (3,4), they write √(32+42) = 3+4 = 7 instead of 5. Another variant: after correctly computing √(25), they write ± 5.

options.text: Make sign errors when coordinates are negative: they write (x₂ - x₁) as (2 - -4) = 2 - 4 = -2 instead of 2 - (-4) = 6.
options.outcome: Another exam-specific error: when finding unknown coordinate from given distance, they square the distance but forget to square the known coordinate difference — e.

options.text: Apply the simplified axis-distance formula |x₂−x₁| or |y₂−y₁| to points where only ONE point lies on an axis (e.
options.outcome: g., (3,0) and (0,4)), or to points on lines parallel to axes but not on the axes (e.

c10_math_ch08.title: Use it in the wild
c10_math_ch08.scenario: In a right triangle, the sine of one acute angle is 5/13. A student claims that the cosine of the other acute angle is also 5/13. Is the student correct?
c10_math_ch08.prompt: You are asked: "Justify your answer using the relationship between the angles and sides of a right triangle" — what do you conclude?

options.text: Yes, the student is correct. sin A = cos C = 5/13 because angles A and C are complementary (sum to 90°), making the opposite side of one angle the adjacent side of the other.
options.outcome: This choice applies the concept to the real situation before acting.

options.text: Confuse "opposite" and "adjacent" when the reference angle is not the standard one (e.
options.outcome: g., angle at the base vs angle at the top).

options.text: Confuse which side is "opposite" and "adjacent" when switching between tan and cot.
options.outcome: For angle θ, tan θ = Opposite/Adjacent, but cot θ = Adjacent/Opposite. In a 3-4-5 triangle with angle θ opposite side 3, tan θ = 3/4, but students write cot θ = 3/4 (same as tan) instead of 4/3.

options.text: Treat "not defined" as a numerical value like 0 or ∞ (infinity).
options.outcome: For example, they write tan 90° = ∞ or cosec 0° = ∞, and then use this "value" in further arithmetic (e.g., tan 90° + cot 90° = ∞ + 0 = ∞).

c10_math_ch09.title: Use it in the wild
c10_math_ch09.scenario: A civil engineer needs to measure the height of a transmission tower without climbing it. She stands 50 m from the base and measures the angle of elevation to the top as 30°. Her eye level is 1.5 m above the ground.
c10_math_ch09.prompt: What is the best explanation or next step?

options.text: (a) Diagram as described. (b) tan 30° = h/50.
options.outcome: (c) Tower height ≈ 30.4 m (including 1.5 m eye level).

options.text: Measure the angle of elevation/depression from the vertical instead of the horizontal.
options.outcome: Another common error: forgetting that the angle of depression from a height equals the angle of elevation from the ground (alternate interior angles), leading to incorrect setups in two-observer problems.

options.text: Draw the horizontal line at the foot of the object (ground level) instead of through the observer's eye, and then mark the angle of elevation at the top of the object (between the vertical and the line of sight).
options.outcome: For example, in a tower problem, they draw the horizontal at the base of the tower and call the angle at the top (between the tower and the line of sight) the angle of elevation.

options.text: Physically place the angle of depression at the wrong vertex — they draw it inside the right triangle at the object's position (ground level) instead of at the observer's eye level.
options.outcome: For example, in a problem "From a 10 m pole, angle of depression of a point is 30°", students draw the 30° angle at the base of the pole (where the right triangle's acute angle is) and label it "angle of depression".

c10_math_ch10.title: Use it in the wild
c10_math_ch10.scenario: A student is asked: "How many tangents can be drawn to a circle of radius 5 cm at a point on its circumference?" The student answers: "Infinite, because you can draw many lines through that point." (a) Identify the error in the student's reasoning.
c10_math_ch10.prompt: What is the best explanation or next step?

options.text: (a) The error is assuming every line through a point on the circle is a tangent. Only the line perpendicular to the radius at that point is a tangent; all other lines through that point are secants (intersecting at two points).
options.outcome: (b) Theorem: At any point on a circle, there exists exactly one tangent.

options.text: Specific error: Students draw a line through a point P on the circle that crosses the circle (enters the interior) and label it a tangent because "it touches at P."
options.outcome: They confuse "passes through a point on the circle" with "intersects the circle at exactly one point."

options.text: Think a chord and a secant are the same thing.
options.outcome: They say "the secant is the segment inside the circle." In exams, they write: "Secant AB = 5 cm" instead of "Chord AB = 5 cm".

options.text: Believe the tangent is perpendicular to the diameter through the point of contact, not the radius.
options.outcome: They draw the diameter through P and mark 90° with the tangent, writing "tangent ⟂ diameter" in proofs.

c10_math_ch11.title: Use it in the wild
c10_math_ch11.scenario: A circular pizza of radius 14 cm is cut into 8 equal slices. One slice is eaten. Find the area of the remaining pizza.
c10_math_ch11.prompt: You are asked: "Explain why the area of one slice is exactly (1/8) of the total area" — what do you conclude?

options.text: 539 cm². The area of one slice is (1/8) of the total because the 8 slices are congruent sectors with equal central angles (45° each), and sector area is proportional to the angle.
options.outcome: This choice applies the concept to the real situation before acting.

options.text: Substitute the diameter d directly into A = π r2 without halving it, computing π d2 instead of π (d/2)2.
options.outcome: For example, with d = 14 cm, they write A = (22/7) × 14 × 14 = 616 cm² instead of the correct 154 cm².

options.text: Confuse the circumference formula C = 2π r with the area formula A = π r2, especially when the radius is a multiple of 7.
options.outcome: For example, given r = 14\,cm, they write C = (22/7) × 142 = 616\,cm (using area formula) instead of C = 2 × (22/7) × 14 = 88\,cm.

options.text: Confuse the denominator in the fraction: they use 180° instead of 360° because they associate circles with 180° (semicircle) or triangle angle sum.
options.outcome: Another specific error: when the angle is given as a fraction of the circle (e.g., "one-third of a circle"), they use the fraction directly as θ (e.

c10_math_ch12.title: Use it in the wild
c10_math_ch12.scenario: A solid toy is in the form of a right circular cylinder with a hemisphere at one end and a cone at the other end. The radius of the common base is 7 cm. The height of the cylindrical part is 10 cm and the height of the conical part is 24 cm.
c10_math_ch12.prompt: You are asked: "Justify your answer with reasoning. (You do not need to compute the numerical value.)" — what do you conclude?

options.text: The student is incorrect. When solids are joined, the surfaces at the joints become internal and are not part of the outer surface area.
options.outcome: The cylinder has two circular faces, the hemisphere has one circular base, and the cone has one circular base.

options.text: The "Add All TSA" Trap: Students mechanically add the total surface area formulas of each individual solid (e.
options.outcome: g., for cylinder+hemisphere: 2πrh + 2πr² + 3πr²) without subtracting the joined faces.

options.text: Use the total height of the solid (cylinder + two hemispheres) directly as 'h' in the formula TSA = 2πr(h + 2r).
options.outcome: For example, if total height = 30 cm and r = 5 cm, they compute TSA = 2π(5)(30 + 10) = 400π instead of first finding h = 30 - 10 = 20 cm, then TSA = 2π(5)(20 + 10) = 300π.

options.text: Confuse "volume of combination" with "surface area of combination" — they subtract overlapping areas in volume problems just like they do for surface area.
options.outcome: For example, when a hemisphere is placed on a cylinder, the circular base of the hemisphere and the top circle of the cylinder coincide. In surface area, we subtract 2πr² (the overlapping circles).

c10_math_ch13.title: Use it in the wild

options.text: (a) The student omitted the alternating signs in cofactor expansion; the correct pattern is +, −, + for R₁. (b) |M| = 0.

options.text: Mishandle the (−1)ⁱ⁺ʲ sign factor when expanding 3×3 determinants.
options.outcome: The exact wrong step: they write the cofactor as +Mᵢⱼ for all positions, or use a fixed alternating pattern (+ − +) regardless of row/column.

c12_math_ch05.title: Use it in the wild
c12_math_ch05.scenario: An electricity board charges ₹5 per unit for the first 100 units, ₹7 per unit for the next 100 units, and ₹10 per unit thereafter. The monthly bill B(x) for x units consumed is B(x) = {cases} 5x, & 0 ≤ x ≤ 100 \\ 500 + 7(x-100), & 100 < x ≤ 200 \\ 1200 + 10(x-200), & x > 200 {cases} Check whether the billing function is continuous at the slab boundaries x = 100 and x = 200.
c12_math_ch05.prompt: You are asked: "Explain what a discontinuity would mean for a consumer" — what do you conclude?

options.text: Continuous at both x = 100 and x = 200. Discontinuity would imply an abrupt, unfair jump in the bill at slab boundaries.

c12_math_ch06.title: Use it in the wild

c12_math_ch07.title: Use it in the wild
c12_math_ch07.scenario: A student claims that tan x\,dx = sec2 x + C because "the derivative of tan x is sec2 x". Identify the error in the student's reasoning and find the correct antiderivative of tan x.
c12_math_ch07.prompt: You are asked: "Explain how you would derive it using a substitution that converts tan x into a form (f'(x)/f(x))" — what do you conclude?

options.text: The student reversed the relationship: derivative of tan x is sec2 x, so antiderivative of sec2 x is tan x + C. The correct antiderivative of tan x is -ln|cos x| + C or ln|sec x| + C.
options.outcome: This choice applies the concept to the real situation before acting.

options.text: Write (1/x)\,dx = ln x + C (without absolute value) because they only consider x > 0.
options.outcome: In, the domain of (1/x) includes negative x, and ln x is undefined for x ≤ 0. The correct antiderivative is ln|x| + C, which works for all x ≠ 0.

options.text: Forget to change the differential dx when substituting.
options.outcome: For example, in ∫ 2x cos(x²) dx, they write u = x² and then ∫ cos u dx, leaving dx instead of replacing with du = 2x dx.

options.text: Write the partial fraction form for a repeated linear factor (x-a)2 as (A/(x-a)2) only, omitting the (B/x-a) term.
options.outcome: For example, for (3x+1/(x-2)2), they set (3x+1/(x-2)2) = (A/(x-2)2), leading to 3x+1 = A, which is impossible. The correct form is (A/x-2) + (B/(x-2)2).

c12_math_ch08.title: Use it in the wild
c12_math_ch08.scenario: A student claims that the area under the curve y = x3 from x = -2 to x = 2 is zero because ∫-22 x3 dx = 0.
c12_math_ch08.prompt: Is the student correct? If not, find the correct area and explain the student's mistake.

options.text: The student is incorrect. The correct area is 8 square units.
options.outcome: The mistake is equating the definite integral (signed area) with geometric area without taking absolute value where the curve is below the axis.

options.text: Think that the definite integral ∫ab f(x) dx always gives the geometric area, even when f(x) is negative on part of the interval.
options.outcome: They write Area = ∫ab f(x) dx without absolute value, leading to negative or zero area for curves that cross the x-axis.

options.text: Compute the area as simply ∫ab f(x) dx without checking if f(x) changes sign.
options.outcome: For example, for y = x3 - 4x on [-2, 2], they might evaluate ∫-22 (x3 - 4x) dx = 0 and conclude the area is 0.

options.text: Write Area = ∫[a to b] [f(x) - g(x)] dx without verifying which function is greater on the interval, and without splitting at intersection points.
options.outcome: For example, with y = x² and y = x on [0, 2], they integrate (x² - x) dx because "x² comes first in the question," getting a negative area.

c12_math_ch09.title: Use it in the wild
c12_math_ch09.scenario: A cup of coffee at 90°C is placed in a room at 20°C. The rate of cooling of the coffee is proportional to the difference between its temperature and the room temperature. (a) Let T be the temperature of the coffee at time t.
c12_math_ch09.prompt: (b) What is the order of this differential equation?

options.text: (a) (dT/dt) = -k(T - 20) (b) Order = 1 (c) The condition T(2)=85 is not an initial condition at t=0; the general solution contains one arbitrary constant which requires the value at t=0 (or any single point) to be fixed. T(2)=85 alone leaves a family of solutions.
options.outcome: This choice applies the concept to the real situation before acting.

options.text: "The order of a differential equation is the highest power (exponent) of the derivative that appears."
options.outcome: Exact wrong step: In ≤ft((d2y/dx2))3 + (dy/dx) = 0, the student sees the exponent 3 on the second derivative and answers "order = 3".

options.text: Confuse "highest power of any derivative" with "highest power of the highest ORDER derivative."
options.outcome: For example, in (d²y/dx²) + (dy/dx)⁴ = 0, they write degree = 4 (taking the power of dy/dx) instead of degree = 1 (power of d²y/dx²).

options.text: "Any function that satisfies the differential equation is a general solution."
options.outcome: Exact error: Students often verify that a given function (e.g., y = x² + 5) satisfies the DE (e.

c12_math_ch10.title: Use it in the wild

options.text: (a) vb = 5j m/s, vr = 3i m/s. Types: perpendicular, coinitial (if same tail), non-zero, non-unit, not equal, not negatives, not collinear.

options.text: Think: "If two vectors have the same magnitude, they are equal."
options.outcome: This is wrong — equality requires BOTH magnitude AND direction.

options.text: Confuse direction ratios with direction cosines.
options.outcome: direction ratios (components). They forget that direction cosines MUST satisfy l2+m2+n2=1 and are ALWAYS the components of a UNIT vector.

options.text: Place vectors tail-to-tail when applying the triangle law, effectively using the parallelogram construction but then taking the wrong diagonal (the one not starting from the common point).

c12_math_ch11.title: Use it in the wild
c12_math_ch11.scenario: A line makes angles 60° and 45° with the positive x-axis and y-axis respectively. Find the possible angles it can make with the positive z-axis.
c12_math_ch11.prompt: You are asked: "Explain why there are two possibilities" — what do you conclude?

options.text: The line makes either 60° or 120° with the positive z-axis.
options.outcome: This choice applies the concept to the real situation before acting.

options.text: Confuse direction ratios with direction cosines.

options.text: Sign errors in Cartesian form numerators: When the Cartesian equation is written as (x - x1/a) = (y - y1/b) = (z - z1/c), students often misread y + 2 as y1 = 2 instead of -2, or z - (-5) as z1 = 5 instead of -5.
options.outcome: They treat the operation in the numerator (addition/subtraction) as the coordinate sign directly.

options.outcome: Students often forget the absolute value because in 2D () the formula tanθ = ≤ft|(m1-m2/1+m1m2)| has absolute value, but the dot product formula in 3D is often memorized without it.

c12_math_ch12.title: Use it in the wild
c12_math_ch12.scenario: A student wrote the following formulation for a problem: "A farmer has 50 acres of land. He grows corn (profit ₹8000/acre) and wheat (profit ₹6000/acre). Corn needs 4 hrs labour/acre, wheat needs 3 hrs labour/acre.
c12_math_ch12.prompt: What is the best explanation or next step?

options.text: The labour constraint is incorrectly written as 4x + 3y ≥ 150. Labour is a limited resource (150 hours available), so the time used cannot exceed availability: 4x + 3y ≤ 150.
options.outcome: This choice applies the concept to the real situation before acting.

options.text: "In a maximisation problem, all constraints must be ≤ type; in a minimisation problem, all constraints must be ≥ type."

c12_math_ch13.title: Use it in the wild
c12_math_ch13.scenario: A survey of 200 students in a school revealed: 120 students play cricket, 80 play football, and 30 play both. A student is selected at random. (a) Find the probability that the student plays cricket given that they play football.

c6_math_ch01.title: Use it in the wild
c6_math_ch01.scenario: You are designing a seating arrangement for 5 students of different heights. Can you arrange them so that no one says '0' when asked to count their taller neighbors?
c6_math_ch01.prompt: You are asked: "Explain your reasoning" — what do you conclude?

options.text: No, it is impossible. The tallest student has no one taller than them, so they must say '0'.
options.outcome: This choice applies the concept to the real situation before acting.

options.text: Believe that "estimation" is just a wild guess with no logical basis.
options.outcome: For example, when asked to estimate the number of breaths in an hour, a student might just say "100" without considering that we breathe roughly 15-20 times per minute.

options.text: Believe that 0 is a natural number because they see it on a number line alongside 1, 2, and 3.
options.outcome: This leads to errors when counting objects or categorizing sets. They forget that natural numbers are strictly for "counting things" (you cannot count "zero" apples in your hand).

options.text: Confuse the digit itself (face value) with its contribution to the total number (place value).
options.outcome: For example, in 3,042, a student might say the place value of 0 is 0, which is correct, but they might struggle with 3,402 and say the 4 is worth 400 because they "see" it near the front, forgetting that the 0 occupies a place that must be accounted for.

c6_math_ch02.title: Use it in the wild
c6_math_ch02.scenario: Imagine a town where the ground level is 0. A shop is at -3, a school is at 1, and a library is at -5. If you are standing at the library, are you closer to the shop or the school?
c6_math_ch02.prompt: You are asked: "Explain your reasoning using the number line" — what do you conclude?

options.text: You are closer to the shop because the distance from -5 to -3 is only 2 units, whereas the distance from -5 to 1 is 6 units.
options.outcome: This choice applies the concept to the real situation before acting.

options.text: Believe that -10 is "bigger" than -1 because 10 is bigger than 1.
options.outcome: This happens because they focus only on the numeral (the magnitude) and ignore the negative sign, which flips the relationship of the numbers.

options.text: Believe that since 5 is bigger than 2, then -5 must be bigger than -2.
options.outcome: They focus on the magnitude of the digit and ignore the negative sign, failing to realize that on the number line, -5 is to the left of -2, making it smaller.

options.text: Treat negative numbers like positive ones, assuming that because 10 is larger than 5, -10 must be larger than -5.
options.outcome: This happens because they see the "10" and "5" and ignore the negative sign, which acts as a "direction" indicator on the number line.

c6_math_ch03.title: Use it in the wild
c6_math_ch03.scenario: If you have a pizza cut into 6 equal slices and another pizza (same size) cut into 12 equal slices, and you eat 3 slices of the first and 6 slices of the second, have you eaten the same amount?
c6_math_ch03.prompt: You are asked: "Explain" — what do you conclude?

options.text: Yes, you have eaten the same amount. 3/6 is half of the pizza, and 6/12 is also half of the pizza.
options.outcome: Even though the slices in the second pizza are smaller, eating 6 of them covers the same total area as eating 3 larger slices from the first pizza.

options.text: Think a larger denominator means a larger fraction (e.
options.outcome: g., thinking 1/8 is bigger than 1/4 because 8 is bigger than 4).

options.text: Try to convert improper fractions to mixed numbers by simply placing the smaller number over the larger number regardless of which was originally the numerator.
options.outcome: For example, converting 8/3 to 3 2/3 instead of 2 2/3. This happens because they focus on "fitting the numbers together" rather than performing the division of the total parts by the denominator.

options.text: Try to find equivalent fractions by adding the same number to both the numerator and denominator (e.
options.outcome: g., changing 1/2 to 2/3).

c6_math_ch04.title: Use it in the wild
c6_math_ch04.scenario: A bottle holds 0.5 litres of water. A cup holds 0.45 litres of juice. Which container holds more liquid?
c6_math_ch04.prompt: How would you explain this to someone who thinks 0.45 is larger because 45 > 5?

options.text: The bottle holds more. Even though 45 is larger than 5, the 5 in 0.5 is in the tenths place (worth 0.50), while the 4 in 0.45 is in the tenths place (worth only 0.40).
options.outcome: Adding a zero makes the comparison clear.

options.text: Think that 0.4 is smaller than 0.25 because they see "4" and "25" and assume 25 is bigger.
options.outcome: They treat the digits after the decimal point as whole numbers rather than parts of a whole (tenths/hundredths).

options.text: Treat the digits to the right of the decimal point as whole numbers, believing that 0.45 is larger than 0.6 because "45 is bigger than 6."
options.outcome: This happens because they ignore the place value (tenths vs. hundredths) and only look at the face value of the digits.

options.text: Think a longer decimal is always larger (e.
options.outcome: g., 0.125 > 0.2) because they treat the decimal part like a whole number, ignoring that the first digit after the decimal point represents tenths, which is the most significant part.

c6_math_ch05.title: Use it in the wild
c6_math_ch05.scenario: You have a piggy bank with ₹100. You add ₹20 every week for 'w' weeks. (a) Write the expression for the total money.
c6_math_ch05.prompt: What is the correct call here — and why?

options.text: (a) 100 + 20w (b) Yes, 20 is a constant because it is the fixed rate of addition.
options.outcome: This choice applies the concept to the real situation before acting.

options.text: Confuse the "coefficient" (the number attached to a variable, like 5 in 5x) with the "variable" itself.
options.outcome: They might say "5x is the variable," when only 'x' is the variable and 5 is a constant acting as a multiplier.

options.text: Mistakenly include the plus or minus sign as a separate "operation" rather than part of the term itself, or they treat the variable as part of the coefficient.
options.outcome: For example, in 5x - 3y, they might identify the coefficient of the second term as 3 instead of -3, or identify 'x' as part of the coefficient 5.

options.text: Confuse the placement of terms in subtraction and division.
options.outcome: For example, when asked for "5 less than x", they write 5 - x instead of x - 5.

c6_math_ch06.title: Use it in the wild
c6_math_ch06.scenario: A factory produces 500 toys in 5 days. The manager wants to know if they can produce 1200 toys in 10 days.
c6_math_ch06.prompt: You are asked: "Using the unitary method, explain if this is possible" — what do you conclude?

options.text: The factory produces 100 toys per day. In 10 days, they would produce 1000 toys.
options.outcome: Therefore, producing 1200 toys is not possible at the current rate.

options.text: Forget to convert units before writing a ratio, or they treat a ratio like a set of independent numbers.
options.outcome: For example, when comparing 1 kg of rice to 500 grams of dal, a student might write 1:500 instead of 1000:500 (or 2:1).

options.text: Try to add the same number to both parts of a ratio to find an equivalent ratio (e.
options.outcome: g., changing 2:3 to 3:4).

options.text: Confuse which number to divide by which.
options.outcome: For example, if 4 pens cost 20 rupees, they might calculate 4 ÷ 20 = 0.2 instead of 20 ÷ 4 = 5. They treat the numbers as isolated digits rather than "Total Cost" and "Total Quantity."

c6_math_ch07.title: Use it in the wild
c6_math_ch07.scenario: A student measures an angle and says it is 150°. Another student says it is 30° because they read the other scale. Is it possible for both to be correct?
c6_math_ch07.prompt: How do you check which one is the correct measure?

options.text: No, only one is correct. You must classify the angle visually first.
options.outcome: If the angle is clearly wider than a right angle (90°), the 150° reading is correct, and the student who read 30° used the wrong scale.

options.text: Confuse a line with a line segment because they see a drawing of a line on a page and assume it is finite because the paper ends.
options.outcome: They think that because they can't see the line extending forever, it must stop at the page edge.

options.text: Believe that if two lines are "close" to each other but don't touch on the paper, they are parallel.
options.outcome: They fail to realize that if they were to extend them, they might cross. For example, they might label two lines that form a very thin 'V' shape as parallel because the gap is small.

options.text: Think the size of an angle changes if you extend the length of the arms.
options.outcome: For example, they might claim that a 30° angle with 5cm arms is smaller than a 30° angle with 10cm arms.

c6_math_ch08.title: Use it in the wild
c6_math_ch08.scenario: Two students, A and B, have different shapes made of 12 equal-length sticks. Student A makes a square. Student B makes a rectangle that is not a square.
c6_math_ch08.prompt: You are asked: "Explain" — what do you conclude?

options.text: Yes, both have the same perimeter because they both use exactly 12 segments of the same length to enclose their respective shapes.
options.outcome: This choice applies the concept to the real situation before acting.

options.text: Add only two sides of a rectangle (length + width) and stop, forgetting that a rectangle has four sides (two lengths and two widths).
options.outcome: They treat the perimeter as the sum of just the dimensions given in the problem statement rather than the full boundary.

options.text: Confuse the formula for perimeter (2 × (l + w)) with the formula for area (l × w).
options.outcome: They attempt to add the dimensions for area or multiply them for perimeter because they treat both formulas as "just some math rule" rather than understanding that perimeter measures lines (edges) and area measures squares (surface).

options.text: Confuse Perimeter (the distance around) with Area (the space inside).
options.outcome: They tend to apply the perimeter formula (2 × (l + w)) when asked for area, or vice-versa, because both involve length and width measurements.

c6_math_ch09.title: Use it in the wild

c6_math_ch09.prompt: What is the correct call here — and why?

options.text: Student B's graph is better because it uses fewer symbols (4 icons vs 8 icons), making it more compact for a small space while still representing the data accurately.
options.outcome: This choice applies the concept to the real situation before acting.

options.text: Fail to "group" tally marks correctly.
options.outcome: When they reach 5, they often continue drawing vertical lines (`|||||`) instead of the standard cross-hatch (`||||` with a strike-through).

options.text: "skip" the diagonal line for the fifth tally, simply drawing five vertical lines (`|||||`).
options.outcome: This makes the data harder to read quickly, as the human eye struggles to distinguish groups of five without that diagonal break.

options.text: Assume every symbol always represents exactly "1" unit, regardless of what the key says.
options.outcome: For example, if the key says one symbol = 10, they will still count the symbols as "1, 2, 3..." instead of "10, 20, 30..."

c6_math_ch10.title: Use it in the wild
c6_math_ch10.scenario: A wind turbine has 3 blades spaced equally. If one blade is painted red, how many rotations does the turbine need to complete for the red blade to return to its original starting position?
c6_math_ch10.prompt: What is the order of symmetry of the turbine blades alone (ignoring the color)?

options.text: The red blade needs a full 360° rotation to return to its exact starting point. However, the turbine structure itself has an order of rotational symmetry of 3, because the blades are identical and spaced equally at 120° intervals.
options.outcome: This choice applies the concept to the real situation before acting.

options.text: Confuse "symmetry" with "congruence" (equal size).
options.outcome: They might think that any shape cut into two equal areas is symmetric.

options.text: Believe that any line that divides a shape into two equal areas is a line of symmetry.
options.outcome: For example, they might think a diagonal of a non-square rectangle is a line of symmetry because it cuts the area in half, failing to check if the two parts are mirror images.

options.text: Confuse "balance" with "symmetry."
options.outcome: They might think a letter like 'S' is symmetric because it looks "balanced" or "pretty," but it doesn't have a line of symmetry because the top half (when folded horizontally) is not a mirror image of the bottom.

c6_math_ch11.title: Use it in the wild
c6_math_ch11.scenario: A friend says that a 40° angle drawn on a small piece of paper is "smaller" than a 40° angle drawn on a large chart paper.
c6_math_ch11.prompt: You are asked: "Explain why your friend is mistaken using the concept of rotation" — what do you conclude?

options.text: Your friend is mistaken because the size of an angle is determined by the amount of rotation at the vertex, not by how long the arms are drawn. Both angles represent the same 40° turn.
options.outcome: This choice applies the concept to the real situation before acting.

options.text: Assume that the size of an angle changes if the length of its arms changes.
options.outcome: They might look at a small angle with long arms and a large angle with short arms and incorrectly label the one with long arms as "bigger."

options.text: Start measuring from the very edge of the ruler (the physical end of the plastic) rather than the '0' mark.
options.outcome: This leads to segments that are consistently shorter or longer than the required length because the ruler's plastic border usually has a gap before the '0' mark starts.

options.text: Mix up the inner and outer scales of the protractor, especially when the ray points to the left.

c6_math_ch12.title: Use it in the wild

c6_math_ch12.prompt: Why is your friend's calculation wrong in the context of a geometric pattern?

options.text: The friend is wrong because they treat each triangle as a separate, isolated shape. In a geometric pattern where triangles are joined, they share sides, so you count fewer sides than if they were isolated.
options.outcome: This choice applies the concept to the real situation before acting.

options.text: Assume all patterns are arithmetic (adding the same number).
options.outcome: For example, in the sequence 1, 2, 4, 8, a student might add 1, then 2, then 4, but then incorrectly assume the next step is adding 5 instead of doubling the increment.

c7_math_ch01.title: Use it in the wild
c7_math_ch01.scenario: A civic body reports that City A has a population of 4,08,200 and City B has a population of 3,99,900. A student claims that City B has a larger population because the digit 9 is larger than the digit 4.
c7_math_ch01.prompt: You are asked: "Analyze this claim, identify the misconception, and determine which city actually has a greater population with mathematical justification" — what do you conclude?

options.text: City A has a greater population. The student's claim is incorrect because place value comparison must always begin from the highest place value (leftmost digit), where 4 lakh is greater than 3 lakh.
options.outcome: This choice applies the concept to the real situation before acting.

options.text: Misplace commas or miscount zeros when writing and reading numbers involving lakhs, writing numbers like 10,0,000 or confusing 1,00,000 with 10,000 because they forget that a lakh requires five zeros following the digit 1 in the Indian system.
options.outcome: Students frequently misplace commas or miscount zeros when writing and reading numbers involving lakhs, writing numbers like 10,0,000 or confusing 1,00,000 with 10,000 because they forget that a lakh requires five zeros following the digit 1 in the Indian system.

c7_math_ch02.title: Use it in the wild
c7_math_ch02.scenario: Consider the arithmetic expression 100 - 10 × 5 + 20 2. A student claims that because there are four numbers, there must be four terms: 100, 10, 5, and 20 2. Is this correct?
c7_math_ch02.prompt: You are asked: "Identify all actual terms in this expression and compute its final value with full reasoning" — what do you conclude?

options.text: The student is incorrect. The expression has 3 terms, not 4, because 10 × 5 forms a single product term.
options.outcome: The correct terms are 100, 50, and 10, giving a final value of 60.

options.text: Split an expression at every single operation symbol (+, -, ×, ÷), treating every number as its own term.
options.outcome: For example, in 20 - 4 × 3, a struggling student might mistakenly think there are three terms (20, 4, and 3) and try to subtract before multiplying.

options.text: Evaluate expressions strictly from left to right across all operation types, ignoring the priority of multiplication and division over addition and subtraction.
options.outcome: For example, when evaluating 10 + 5 × 2, a student incorrectly adds 10 + 5 = 15 first, then multiplies by 2 to get 30, instead of multiplying 5 × 2 = 10 first and then adding 10 + 10 = 20.

options.text: Evaluate expressions strictly from left to right across the entire string without respecting brackets or the order of operations, leading to incorrect comparisons.
options.outcome: For example, when comparing 10 + 2 × 5 and (10 + 2) × 5, a student might incorrectly calculate the left side as (10 + 2) × 5 = 60 by rushing or adding first, missing that multiplication must occur before addition.

c7_math_ch03.title: Use it in the wild
c7_math_ch03.scenario: A carpenter needs to cut a wooden plank of length 6 meters. His measuring tape only has markings for whole meters and markings dividing each meter into 10 equal smaller parts. The carpenter measures a required length of 4 whole meters and 12 small parts of a meter.
c7_math_ch03.prompt: You are asked: "Explain why writing this as 4(12/10) meters is problematic in terms of unit notation, and show the correct way to express this measurement by converting excess small parts into whole meters" — what do you conclude?

options.text: Writing 4(12/10) is problematic because a fractional part attached to a mixed number should represent a proper fraction (less than 1 whole unit). Since 12 small parts contain a full group of 10, those 10 parts form 1 new whole meter.
options.outcome: Adding this to the 4 meters gives 5 whole meters and (2/10) of a meter, written correctly as 5(2/10) meters.

options.text: Treat the smaller fractional parts (tenths, hundredths) as independent whole numbers rather than parts of a whole, leading them to write 3 strips and 4 parts as 34 instead of 3(4/10).
options.outcome: Another common error is believing that because 100 is greater than 10, a hundredth ((1/100)) is larger than a tenth ((1/1010)), ignoring the inverse relationship between the number of partitions and the size of each part.

options.text: Write the fraction (1/10) as decimal 0.01 instead of 0.1.
options.outcome: This happens because they confuse the tenths place (the first position after the decimal point) with the hundredths place, thinking that the number of zeros in the denominator (10 has one zero) does not correspond directly to the decimal place value structure.

options.text: Misinterpret the place value of zeros in decimals, writing (6/100) as 0.6 instead of 0.06.
options.outcome: They treat the numerator 6 as if it belongs directly next to the decimal point, ignoring the empty tenths place that requires a zero placeholder.

c7_math_ch04.title: Use it in the wild
c7_math_ch04.scenario: Amit says that in the expression 3m + 4, the letter m can be replaced by any integer, including negative integers. Sneha argues that m can only represent positive counting numbers because you cannot have a negative number of objects in real life.
c7_math_ch04.prompt: You are asked: "Evaluate both arguments based on the mathematical definition of a variable in algebra" — what do you conclude?

options.text: Amit is mathematically correct in a general algebraic context because a variable can represent positive integers, negative integers, zero, or fractions. However, Sneha is right if the variable specifically counts physical objects (like people or books) in a real-world scenario.

options.text: Drop the negative sign when identifying coefficients of terms that follow a subtraction sign, or they confuse the constant term with coefficients.
options.outcome: For example, in the expression 3x2 - 5x + 7, a student will often say the coefficient of x is 5 instead of -5, ignoring the minus sign that belongs to the term.

options.text: Distribute a multiplier to only the first term inside parentheses or fail to distribute a negative sign correctly across all terms.
options.outcome: For example, when simplifying -2(3x - 4), students frequently write -6x - 4 instead of the correct -6x + 8, forgetting that multiplying a negative number by a negative number yields a positive product.

c7_math_ch05.title: Use it in the wild

options.text: Disagree with the engineer. Two straight lines can only intersect at a single point because if they crossed at two points, at least one of the lines would have to curve or bend, violating the definition of straight lines.

options.text: Confuse the linear pair sum property (180^°) with complementary angles (90^°) or full-turn angles (360^°).

c7_math_ch06.title: Use it in the wild

c7_math_ch06.prompt: You are asked: "Explain how their methods relate to each other" — what do you conclude?

options.text: Both students are correct. Amit uses recursive differences (adding consecutive odd numbers), while Priya uses an explicit positional formula (n2).

c7_math_ch07.title: Use it in the wild

options.text: No, triangle XYZ will not be an equilateral triangle. For a triangle to be equilateral, all three sides must be equal in length.

c7_math_ch08.title: Use it in the wild
c7_math_ch08.scenario: Two students, Amit and Sneha, are trying to solve (4/9) × (3/8). Amit multiplies straight across to get (12/72) and then simplifies. Sneha simplifies the fractions diagonally before multiplying, cancelling 4 with 8 and 3 with 9, to get (1/3) × (1/2).

options.text: Rahul is incorrect. While the outer side lengths are equal, a star shape's overall geometry depends heavily on its interior and re-entrant angles.

options.outcome: They write 372 as 3 (hundreds), 7 (tens), 2 (units) in vertical rows, forgetting that the place values are 1, 20, 400, 8000, not 1, 10, 100.

options.text: Think the digit shapes were invented at once by Arabs (hence "Arabic numerals") and that zero was always a circle.
options.outcome: The exact wrong step: they see the modern printed forms and assume they were designed that way, not realizing the shapes came from cursive handwriting of Indian scribes (e.

c8_math_ch04.title: Use it in the wild
c8_math_ch04.scenario: Rahul draws a four-sided figure and measures its angles: 100°, 80°, 100°, 70°. He says, "This cannot be a quadrilateral because opposite angles are not equal." Is Rahul correct?
c8_math_ch04.prompt: You are asked: "Explain why or why not, using the definition and angle sum property" — what do you conclude?

options.text: Rahul is correct that it's not a quadrilateral, but for the wrong reason. The angle sum is 350°, not 360°, so it violates the fundamental property.
options.outcome: Opposite angles need not be equal in a general quadrilateral — only in parallelograms.

options.text: Think a quadrilateral must look "regular" like a rectangle or square.
options.outcome: They reject irregular shapes (e.g., a quadrilateral with sides 3 cm, 5 cm, 4 cm, 6 cm and no parallel sides) as "not quadrilaterals."

options.text: Confuse "diagonals bisect each other" with "diagonals are equal" (rectangle) or "diagonals are perpendicular" (rhombus).
options.outcome: In a general parallelogram, diagonals are NOT necessarily equal or perpendicular. They only share the midpoint.

options.text: Think "kite = rhombus" and apply rhombus properties: they assume both diagonals bisect each other, both diagonals are perpendicular bisectors, and all sides are equal.
options.outcome: For example, given a kite with sides 5 cm, 5 cm, 8 cm, 8 cm, a student might say "all sides are 5 cm" or "both diagonals cut each other in half" — confusing the specific adjacent-pair equality with the rhombus's all-sides-equal and parallelogram's bisecting diagonals.

c8_math_ch05.title: Use it in the wild
c8_math_ch05.scenario: Without adding, determine whether the sum of the numbers from 101 to 110 (ten consecutive numbers) is odd or even. Then determine if it is a multiple of 5.
c8_math_ch05.prompt: You are asked: "Explain your reasoning for both" — what do you conclude?

options.text: The sum is odd and a multiple of 5.
options.outcome: This choice applies the concept to the real situation before acting.

options.text: Believe that the sum of k consecutive numbers is always a multiple of k.
options.outcome: They test k=2 (sum is odd, not multiple of 2), k=3 (multiple of 3), k=4 (not multiple of 4), and incorrectly generalise that it works for odd k only. The exact error: they write n+(n+1)+...

options.text: Write the reversed number as a+b (sum of digits) or 10a+b (same as original) instead of 10b+a.
options.outcome: They treat digits as values to be added rather than place-value positions. For example, for number 37, they write reversal as 3+7=10 or 10×3+7=37, not 10×7+3=73.

options.text: Treat cryptarithms as trial-and-error guessing games, randomly assigning digits to letters and checking if the arithmetic works.
options.outcome: They fail to recognize that well-constructed cryptarithms have a UNIQUE solution that can be reached through pure logical deduction — each step eliminates possibilities until only one assignment remains.

c8_math_ch06.title: Use it in the wild
c8_math_ch06.scenario: Ravi calculated 19 × 24 by writing 19 × 24 = 19 × (20 + 4) = 19 × 20 + 19 × 4 = 380 + 76 = 456. Priya did 19 × 24 = (20 - 1) × 24 = 20 × 24 - 1 × 24 = 480 - 24 = 456. Both used the distributive property.
c8_math_ch06.prompt: You are asked: "Justify your choice" — what do you conclude?

options.text: Both are valid because subtraction is adding a negative, so distributive property over addition covers both.
options.outcome: This choice applies the concept to the real situation before acting.

options.text: Write a(b + c) = ab + c (forgetting to multiply the outside term by the second inside term) or a(b + c) = ab + ac but then make sign errors with negatives like -2(x + 3) = -2x + 6 (forgetting -2 × 3 = -6).
options.outcome: With fractions/decimals, they might distribute only the whole number part: 2.5(4 + 2) = 2.5 × 4 + 2 (treating 2.5 as 2 and 0.5 separately but incorrectly).

options.text: Treat the negative term in a binomial (e.
options.outcome: g., x - 3) as a positive length in the area model, drawing a rectangle of width 3 instead of representing it as a removal of a 3-unit strip.

options.text: Write (2x+3)² = 4x² + 9, completely omitting the middle term 12x.
options.outcome: They treat squaring a binomial as squaring each term individually, ignoring the distributive property that generates the cross term 2ab.

c8_math_ch07.title: Use it in the wild
c8_math_ch07.scenario: A school has 400 students and 20 teachers (ratio 20:1). The principal wants to maintain this ratio. Next year, 60 new students enroll.
c8_math_ch07.prompt: Are both methods always equivalent? Test with a different number of new students (e.g., 100 new students) and explain."

options.text: Both methods yield the same result because maintaining a fixed ratio (20:1) inherently requires multiplicative scaling. The admin's "add 3 teachers" is the outcome of the multiplicative factor (460/400 = 1.15).
options.outcome: They are not different approaches; one describes the increment, the other describes the scaling factor.

options.text: Treat proportional situations additively: they add the same absolute amount to both quantities in a ratio (e.
options.outcome: g., changing 2:3 to 4:5 by adding 2) believing this preserves the relationship.

options.text: Treat scaling as additive: they believe that to enlarge an image, you add the same amount to both width and height.
options.outcome: For example, given a 12 cm × 8 cm image and a target width of 18 cm, they compute 18 − 12 = 6, then add 6 to the height to get 14 cm, instead of finding the scale factor 18/12 = 1.5 and multiplying 8 × 1.5 = 12 cm.

options.text: Treat the ratio a:b as just two numbers written with a colon, ignoring that (1) the quantities must be in identical units before forming the ratio, and (2) the order a:b is not interchangeable – a:b is the multiplicative comparison a/b, so 3:5 means 0.6 while 5:3 means 1.67.
options.outcome: They also confuse part-part ratios (e.g., boys:girls) with part-whole ratios (e.

c8_math_ch08.title: Use it in the wild
c8_math_ch08.scenario: A bowl contains 20 red marbles and 30 blue marbles. If 10 more red marbles are added, does the percentage of red marbles increase, decrease, or stay the same?
c8_math_ch08.prompt: You are asked: "Justify your answer without calculating the exact percentage" — what do you conclude?

options.text: The percentage of red marbles increases. Originally red was 2/5 (40%) of the marbles; after adding only red marbles, red becomes 1/2 (50%) of the marbles.
options.outcome: Adding to the numerator only (part) while the denominator (whole) also increases but by a smaller proportion raises the fraction.

options.text: Treat % as a unit label (like "cm" or "kg") rather than an operator meaning "divided by 100".
options.outcome: For example, they write 0.5% = 0.5 (dropping the % but keeping the value) or think 120% is impossible because "you can't have more than 100%".

options.text: Use the time value directly without converting months to years (e.
options.outcome: g., using T=6 for 6 months instead of T=0.5) OR they forget to divide by 100 when the rate is a percentage (e.

options.text: Calculate discount percentage on the selling price instead of the marked price.
options.outcome: For example, if marked price = ₹1000, selling price = ₹850, they compute discount % = (150 ÷ 850) × 100 ≈ 17.6% instead of (150 ÷ 1000) × 100 = 15%.

c8_math_ch09.title: Use it in the wild
c8_math_ch09.scenario: A square tile has side 20 cm. A mason wants to cut a larger square tile of exactly double the area from a rectangular slab, using only a rope (no calculator). He knows the Sulba-Sutra method.
c8_math_ch09.prompt: (c) Why would marking 28.3 cm on the rope (using a calculator) be less reliable than the rope method?

options.text: (a) 20√2 cm (exact rope length). (b) The new square comprises 4 congruent right isosceles triangles; the original comprises 2 — area ratio 4:2 = 2:1 exactly.
options.outcome: (c) Decimal approximation (28.3 cm) rounds the irrational √2, causing area error; the rope uses the exact geometric length.

options.text: Believe doubling the side length of a square doubles its area (e.
options.outcome: g., side 5 cm → side 10 cm for double area).

options.text: Forget to identify the longest side first and instead arbitrarily pick two sides to square and add, comparing with the square of the third side.
options.outcome: For example, given sides 6, 8, 10, they might check 62 + 102 = 82 (36+100=136 vs 64) and incorrectly conclude it is not right-angled.

options.text: Think that to double the area of a square, they should double the side length.
options.outcome: four times 16.

c8_math_ch10.title: Use it in the wild
c8_math_ch10.scenario: In a school, the ratio of teachers to students is 1:25. If there are 1200 students, how many teachers are needed? The principal decides to improve the ratio to 1:20.
c8_math_ch10.prompt: You are asked: "How many additional teachers must be hired? Solve using cross-multiplication for both parts" — what do you conclude?

options.text: 48 teachers currently needed; 12 additional teachers must be hired (total 60).
options.outcome: This choice applies the concept to the real situation before acting.

options.text: Multiply the two numerators together and the two denominators together (a×c = b×d) instead of cross-multiplying (a×d = b×c).
options.outcome: For example, in 3/5 = x/20, they write 3x = 5×20 = 100 instead of 3×20 = 5x. This happens because they see "multiply across" visually as horizontal lines rather than diagonal crosses.

options.text: Mechanically apply the direct proportion formula x1/y1 = x2/y2 to every problem with two quantities, even when the relationship is inverse (e.
options.outcome: g., workers-days, speed-time).

options.text: Write RF as 1:4000 for "1 cm = 4 km" by converting 4 km to 4000 m and pairing 1 cm with 4000 m.
options.outcome: They ignore that the map unit (cm) and ground unit (m) are different, so the ratio is not unitless. The exact wrong step: 4 km → 4000 m → RF = 1:4000, instead of 4 km → 400,000 cm → RF = 1:400,000.

c8_math_ch11.title: Use it in the wild
c8_math_ch11.scenario: The Koch snowflake (which you will study later) starts with an equilateral triangle. At each step, every straight segment is replaced by a 4-segment zigzag (generator) that is 4/3 times longer. (a) If the initial triangle has side 9 cm, what is the perimeter after step 1?
c8_math_ch11.prompt: You are asked: "Justify using the idea of self-similarity and scaling" — what do you conclude?

options.text: (a) Step 1: 36 cm; Step 2: 48 cm. (b) The generator (4-segment zigzag) is the fundamental unit; the curve at any step is composed of scaled copies of the generator, and the generator itself contains smaller copies — exact self-similarity across all scales.
options.outcome: (c) Yes, possible.

options.text: Confuse self-similarity with symmetry (mirror or rotational).
options.outcome: They see a fern and say "it's symmetric" because the left and right sides look alike, but the defining feature is scale similarity, not mirror symmetry.

options.text: Count the curved surface of a cylinder or cone as a "face" because they think any surface is a face.
options.outcome: They also miscount edges on pyramids by counting the slant edges twice (once for each adjacent triangle) or by counting the base perimeter edges separately from the lateral edges.

options.text: Incorrectly count edges and vertices on polyhedra drawn in 2D (on paper) because they miss hidden edges or double-count visible ones.
options.outcome: For example, on a cube drawn as a net or oblique sketch, they may count only 9 edges (the visible ones) instead of 12, or count the "back" vertex twice.

c8_math_ch12.title: Use it in the wild
c8_math_ch12.scenario: A teacher gives a quiz to 8 students. The scores (out of 20) are: 12, 14, 15, 16, 16, 18, 19, and one score is missing. The teacher knows the class mean is 16.
c8_math_ch12.prompt: What is the best explanation or next step?

options.outcome: Missing deviation must be +2.

options.text: Think the mean is simply the "middle number" (confusing it with the median) and therefore assume the balancing property means there are an equal number of points on each side.
options.outcome: They might verify by counting points instead of summing distances.

options.text: Believe the mean is always the "best" average because it is the most commonly used and uses all data points.
options.outcome: They fail to recognise that in skewed distributions (e.g., income data with a few very high earners) the mean gets pulled toward the tail and no longer represents the typical value.

options.text: Confuse range with the "number of values" in the data set (e.
options.outcome: g., for data {4, 7, 9}, they say range = 3 because there are three numbers).

c8_math_ch13.title: Use it in the wild
c8_math_ch13.scenario: Your friend shows you this trick: "Think of a number. Double it. Add 8.
c8_math_ch13.prompt: You are asked: "Explain each step of your reasoning" — what do you conclude?

options.text: Yes, your friend is correct. The algebraic simplification shows the final expression is always 7, independent of x.
options.outcome: The operations "double then add 8 then divide by 2" are equivalent to "add 4" (since 8/2 = 4), and adding 3 more gives 7 before subtracting the original number.

options.text: Write the algebraic expression incorrectly when a multiplication step follows an addition step.
options.outcome: For example, in "Think of a number. Add 5.

options.text: Translate "5 less than x" as 5 - x instead of x - 5.
options.outcome: For example, in "Ravi has 5 less than twice the number of pens Shyam has," they write 5 - 2x instead of 2x - 5.

options.text: Define the variable for "consecutive even/odd numbers" as x, x+1, x+2 instead of x, x+2, x+4.
options.outcome: For example, for "sum of 3 consecutive even numbers is 72", they write x + (x+1) + (x+2) = 72 → 3x + 3 = 72 → x = 23, giving 23, 24, 25 (not even!)

c8_math_ch14.title: Use it in the wild
c8_math_ch14.scenario: A farmer has a rectangular field 120 m long and 80 m wide. He wants to divide it into two equal rectangles by building a fence parallel to the width. What is the area of each smaller rectangle?
c8_math_ch14.prompt: If fencing costs ₹50 per metre, what is the total cost?

options.text: Area of each smaller rectangle = 4800 m². Length of new fence = 80 m.
options.outcome: Total cost = ₹4000.

options.text: Multiply length and width given in different units (e.
options.outcome: g., metres and centimetres) without converting, producing an answer with mixed units like "1500 m cm" or incorrectly labelling it m².

options.text: Draw a diagonal that creates a trapezoid or an irregular quadrilateral instead of a triangle and rectangle, then stall because they lack a formula for that shape.
options.outcome: Alternatively, when a triangle is formed, they incorrectly use a slanted side length as the height instead of dropping a perpendicular to the chosen base.

options.text: Use any side length as "height" instead of the perpendicular height.
options.outcome: For example, given a triangle with sides 5 cm, 12 cm, 13 cm (right triangle), they might take base = 12 and height = 13 (the hypotenuse) and compute (1/2) × 12 × 13 = 78 cm², instead of using the two legs (5 and 12) as base and height to get 30 cm².

c9_math_ch01.title: Use it in the wild
c9_math_ch01.scenario: A city planner uses a coordinate grid for a new township. The town hall is at (0, 0). The main road runs along the x-axis (East-West), and the central avenue runs along the y-axis (North-South).
c9_math_ch01.prompt: (c) If a library is to be built exactly halfway between the park and the school, what are its coordinates?

options.text: (a) Park: North-West; School: South-East. (b) Yes, Quadrant II and Quadrant IV are opposite.
options.outcome: (c) Library at (1, 1).

options.text: Confuse the order of coordinates and write (y, x) instead of (x, y), especially when the point is in the first quadrant where both numbers are positive.
options.outcome: For example, they plot (3, 5) by going 3 up and 5 right because they think "first number is vertical".

options.text: Assume that if the three distances AB, BC, AC are all different, the points cannot be collinear.
options.outcome: They incorrectly think collinearity requires two equal distances (i.e., one point is the midpoint).

options.text: Write the formula as (1/2) [x1(y2 - y3) + x2(y3 - y1) + x3(y1 - y2)] without the absolute value bars, and then get a negative area for clockwise-ordered vertices.
options.outcome: They also frequently mess up the cyclic order, writing x1(y3 - y2) instead of x1(y2 - y3), which changes the sign but not the magnitude.

c9_math_ch02.title: Use it in the wild
c9_math_ch02.scenario: A student writes the linear polynomial for "5 less than 3 times a number x" as 5 - 3x. Another student writes it as 3x - 5. Which student is correct?
c9_math_ch02.prompt: You are asked: "Explain the reasoning, and write the correct polynomial in standard form" — what do you conclude?

options.text: The second student is correct: "5 less than 3 times x" = 3x - 5. Standard form: 3x - 5.
options.outcome: The expression 5 - 3x is also a linear polynomial (standard form: -3x + 5) but represents a different situation, e.

options.text: Think that any expression with x in it is a linear polynomial.
options.outcome: For example, they classify (1/x) + 2, x2 + 3x, √(x) + 5, or (2x+1/x-1) as linear polynomials because they "see an x."

options.text: Write the equation for "total time" in distance-speed-time problems as (distance1 + distance2) / (speed1 + speed2) = total time, instead of distance1/speed1 + distance2/speed2 = total time.
