c8_physics_ch01.title: Use it in the wild
c8_physics_ch01.scenario: A student writes this question for a science fair project: "How does the colour of light affect the temperature of water in a beaker?" She plans to use red, blue, and green cellophane filters over identical lamps shining on identical beakers with 100 mL water at 25°C for 20 minutes.
c8_physics_ch01.prompt: You are asked: "Identify TWO flaws in the variable structure of this investigation and explain how to fix each flaw to make it a fair test" — what do you conclude?

options.text: Flaw 1: Filters change both wavelength AND intensity → not a fair test of colour alone. Fix: Equalize transmitted power (W) for each colour using a lux/power meter and voltage adjustment.
options.outcome: Flaw 2: Categorical independent variable (red/blue/green) prevents quantitative relationship analysis.

options.text: Believe a focused question is just a "more detailed" version of a broad question — they add adjectives ("How does the hot temperature affect...?")
options.outcome: but still fail to structure it as a relationship between ONE changed factor and ONE measured factor while holding others constant.

options.text: Treat the overview as a mere list of chapter names to memorize, missing that each topic is an invitation to apply the same investigative toolkit (questions, variables, evidence, iteration) they just learned.
options.outcome: They also assume biology topics require only memorization while physics topics require math, not realizing that Microorganisms demands careful variable-controlled culturing and Light demands precise angle measurement—both are quantitative investigations.

options.text: Think "observation" means only looking with eyes, and "experiment" means any hands-on activity (e.
options.outcome: g., making a volcano with baking soda).

c8_physics_ch02.title: Use it in the wild
c8_physics_ch02.scenario: Two bulbs, A (incandescent) and B (CFL), are connected to identical batteries in separate circuits. Bulb A draws 0.5 A at 12 V and produces 3 W of light. Bulb B draws 0.1 A at 12 V and produces 2.5 W of light.
c8_physics_ch02.prompt: You are asked: "Justify with calculations" — what do you conclude?

options.text: Bulb A efficiency = 50%. Bulb B's given data implies 208% efficiency, which is impossible.
options.outcome: The data for Bulb B must be incorrect (light output cannot exceed electrical input).

options.text: Believe the wire itself becomes a permanent magnet when current flows, and that the compass needle is attracted to the wire like iron filings to a magnet.

options.text: Think a bulb with higher wattage is always "more powerful" and therefore better, not realizing wattage indicates electrical energy consumption rate, not light output.
options.outcome: They believe a 100 W incandescent bulb is superior to a 20 W CFL because 100 > 20, ignoring that the CFL can produce similar brightness with far less energy.

options.text: Believe that any "dead" battery can be revived by putting it in a charger, or that rechargeable batteries last forever.
options.outcome: They confuse recharging (reversing the reaction) with replenishing (adding chemicals), and they overlook that every rechargeable chemistry has a finite cycle life (e.

c8_physics_ch03.title: Use it in the wild
c8_physics_ch03.scenario: A student says: "When I hold a 1 kg book stationary in my hand, I am not applying any force because the book is not moving." Is the student correct?
c8_physics_ch03.prompt: You are asked: "Explain using the concept of force as a push or pull" — what do you conclude?

options.text: The student is incorrect. The hand exerts an upward push (force) of about 10 N to balance the downward gravitational pull.
options.outcome: Force does not require motion; it requires interaction.

options.text: Believe "force is something an object has" (like a property) rather than an interaction between objects — e.
options.outcome: g., they say "the ball has force because it's moving" or "the book on the table has no force because it's not moving."

options.text: "smoother surfaces always have less friction" and that polishing metal surfaces to a mirror finish will minimize friction.
options.outcome: extremely smooth clean metal surfaces in vacuum exhibit HIGHER friction due to increased adhesive forces (cold welding) and greater real contact area.

options.text: Believe "heavier objects fall faster" because they feel a heavier object pulls harder on their hand.
options.outcome: They conflate the magnitude of gravitational force (which is larger for larger mass) with the resulting acceleration, forgetting Newton's second law (a = F/m) which they will learn later.

c8_physics_ch04.title: Use it in the wild
c8_physics_ch04.scenario: A block of weight 200 N rests on a table with its base area 0.5 m². A student places an identical block on top of it. What happens to the pressure on the table?
c8_physics_ch04.prompt: You are asked: "Explain using the pressure formula" — what do you conclude?

options.text: The pressure doubles from 400 Pa to 800 Pa because pressure is directly proportional to force when area is constant.
options.outcome: This choice applies the concept to the real situation before acting.

options.text: Believe pressure and force are interchangeable terms — they say "I applied a lot of pressure" when they mean "I pushed hard."
options.outcome: They think a larger force always means larger pressure, ignoring that spreading the same force over a larger area (like lying on a bed of nails) reduces pressure.

options.text: Believe the "eye" of a cyclone is a region of high pressure because it's calm and clear.
options.outcome: the entire cyclone is a low-pressure system; the eye has the lowest surface pressure.

options.text: Think "cyclone safety = only evacuation to shelter."
options.outcome: increases internal pressure and roof lift-off risk.

c8_physics_ch05.title: Use it in the wild
c8_physics_ch05.scenario: A sealed syringe contains 10 mL of water and 5 mL of air at 25°C. The plunger is pushed in, reducing the air volume to 2.5 mL while temperature stays constant.

options.text: Dissolved oxygen concentration doubles (increases by factor of 2).
options.outcome: This choice applies the concept to the real situation before acting.

options.text: Believe "the solute is always the solid and the solvent is always the liquid" because most classroom examples are solid-in-liquid (salt water, sugar water).

options.outcome: They miss that gas dissolution is exothermic (releases heat), so by Le Chatelier's principle, adding heat shifts equilibrium toward the reactant (gas) side, decreasing solubility.

options.outcome: This leads to errors in gas-in-liquid solutions (e.g., claiming water is the solute in soda because CO₂ is "added") and solid solutions (e.

c8_physics_ch06.title: Use it in the wild
c8_physics_ch06.scenario: A student places a convex lens of focal length 12 cm in contact with a concave lens of focal length 18 cm. Without using the lens formula, predict whether the combination will behave as a converging or diverging lens.
c8_physics_ch06.prompt: You are asked: "Justify your answer by comparing the power of each lens" — what do you conclude?

options.text: The combination will behave as a converging lens because the convex lens has greater power (shorter focal length magnitude) than the concave lens, resulting in a positive net power.
options.outcome: This choice applies the concept to the real situation before acting.

options.text: Believe the name "concave" or "convex" describes the overall shape of the mirror object (e.
options.outcome: g., the glass bulges out, so it's convex) rather than the reflecting surface itself.

options.text: Think a concave lens "always forms a virtual image" is its defining property, but they confuse this with the fact that a convex lens can also form virtual images when the object is within the focal length.
options.outcome: They also mistakenly believe the focal length of a lens is half its radius of curvature (as in mirrors), not realizing the lens-maker's formula involves refractive index and two surfaces.

options.text: Think the ray through the optical centre always passes straight without any lateral shift, even for thick lenses.
options.outcome: In we assume thin lenses where this shift is negligible, but they incorrectly apply this to all lenses and also believe the ray bends at the centre plane rather than passing straight through the geometric centre.

c8_physics_ch07.title: Use it in the wild

options.text: No, the last week of March 2025 does not have a Full Moon. The Full Moon is on March 14 (mid-month).

options.outcome: This causes predictions to drift by 1.5 days per month.

c8_physics_ch08.title: Use it in the wild

c8_physics_ch09.title: Use it in the wild
c8_physics_ch09.scenario: A new exoplanet "Kepler-186f" is discovered. It orbits a red dwarf star at a distance where it receives 32% of Earth's solar flux. Its radius is 1.1× Earth's, mass 1.4× Earth's.
c8_physics_ch09.prompt: You are asked: "List two additional conditions (beyond distance/flux) that must be met for surface liquid water, and explain how the planet's higher mass helps or hinders each" — what do you conclude?

options.text: Habitable zone = distance range where stellar flux allows liquid water given an Earth-like atmosphere. Two additional conditions: (1) Atmospheric pressure > 0.6 kPa (triple point of water) — higher mass helps by increasing gravity (≈1.16g), improving gas retention.
options.outcome: (2) Greenhouse gas concentration sufficient to raise temperature from -40°C (estimated for 32% flux) to >0°C — higher mass helps retain CO₂ but may hinder if it also retains H/He envelope preventing rocky surface.

options.text: Think "Earth is at the right distance from the Sun, so it has the right temperature for life" — treating distance as the sole determinant.
options.outcome: They ignore that without an atmosphere, Earth's average temperature would be -18°C (calculated from radiative equilibrium), freezing all water. The actual +15°C comes from the greenhouse effect.

options.text: Believe that a satellite "takes a photograph" exactly like a smartphone camera – capturing a single snapshot of the whole Earth in natural colour at high resolution.
options.outcome: most Earth observation satellites use push-broom scanners (linear detector arrays) that build an image line-by-line as the satellite moves, they capture data in separate spectral bands (not a single RGB shot), and the raw data is radiometrically and geometrically corrected on the ground before becoming a usable image.

options.text: Think "self-sustaining" means "unchanging" or "indestructible" — they imagine Earth's cycles are like a perpetual motion machine that will always return to the exact same state regardless of human impact.
options.outcome: Specifically, they believe the water cycle will always bring rain to the same places, or that planting a few trees instantly cancels out fossil fuel emissions, because they confuse dynamic equilibrium (fluctuating around a stable average) with static stability (fixed, rigid state).

c9_physics_ch01.title: Use it in the wild
c9_physics_ch01.scenario: A student reads in a newspaper: "Scientists have proven that drinking coffee prevents cancer." The article cites a study where 10,000 coffee drinkers had 20% lower cancer rates than non-drinkers. Using your understanding of systematic science, explain why the headline "proven" is scientifically inaccurate.
c9_physics_ch01.prompt: You are asked: "Identify two confounding variables the study should have controlled, and describe how a systematic follow-up investigation would be designed" — what do you conclude?

options.text: The headline is inaccurate because: (1) Science does not "prove" — it corroborates through failed falsification attempts; one observational study cannot establish causation.
options.outcome: (3) Systematic follow-up: RCT with falsifiable hypothesis, double-blind randomization, controlled confounders, pre-registration, independent replication — meeting falsifiability, control, and communal verification criteria.

options.text: Believe "systematic" only means "step-by-step procedure" (like following a lab manual).
options.outcome: They miss that systematic in science primarily means communally regulated: claims are subjected to intersubjective scrutiny (peer review), must be reproducible by independent agents, and are structured to be falsifiable — not just personally orderly.

options.text: Think "science impacts society only through big inventions like rockets or smartphones" and overlook how fundamental principles (e.
options.outcome: g., pressure in a pressure cooker, friction in brakes, convex mirrors in traffic) permeate daily objects.

options.text: Think rest and motion are absolute — a body is "really" at rest or "really" in motion.
options.outcome: The exact error: they do not specify the reference frame and assume there is a "true" state of rest or motion.

c9_physics_ch02.title: Use it in the wild
c9_physics_ch02.scenario: A particle moves along the x-axis. Its position at different times is: t=0 s, x=0 m; t=2 s, x=5 m; t=4 s, x=2 m; t=6 s, x=8 m. c9_physics_ch02.prompt: You are asked: "Justify using distance and displacement concepts" — what do you conclude?

options.text: Both average speed and magnitude of average velocity are greatest in the interval 4-6 s (distance = 6 m, |displacement| = 6 m). In 0-2 s both are 5 m/2s; in 2-4 s both are 3 m/2s.
options.outcome: This choice applies the concept to the real situation before acting.

options.text: Think displacement is "distance with a direction sign" and calculate it by adding signed segment lengths (e.
options.outcome: g., +5 for east, -3 for west) but then take the absolute value of the sum, missing that displacement is the vector from start to end, not the algebraic sum of signed distances.

options.text: Believe a real "centrifugal force" pushes the object outward during circular motion.
options.outcome: They argue: "When I sit in a car taking a sharp turn, I feel pushed outward, so there must be an outward force."

options.text: Treat the three equations of motion as interchangeable recipes: they pick the one that contains the unknown they want, without checking whether all the other variables in that equation are known.
options.outcome: For example, given u, a, and t, they might try to use v² = u² + 2as to find s, not realizing v is also unknown. This leads to circular reasoning or incorrect substitution.

c9_physics_ch03.title: Use it in the wild
c9_physics_ch03.scenario: "Newton's First Law is just a special case of the Second Law (F = ma) when F = 0 and a = 0."
c9_physics_ch03.prompt: You are asked: "Evaluate this statement by explaining whether the First Law is independent of the Second Law or derivable from it, and why the First Law is considered a fundamental principle in its own right" — what do you conclude?

options.text: The statement is mathematically correct but conceptually incomplete. Mathematically, if F = 0 in F = ma, then a = 0, meaning velocity is constant (rest or uniform motion) — so the First Law follows from the Second Law when F = 0.
options.outcome: However, the First Law is conceptually independent and fundamental for three reasons: (1) It defines what a force is — a cause of change in motion.

options.text: Think a force is needed to keep an object moving.
options.outcome: The exact error: they observe that moving objects in everyday life stop on their own and conclude that force is needed to sustain motion.

options.text: Believe the resultant force is simply the arithmetic sum of all force magnitudes, ignoring direction.
options.outcome: For example, they add 10 N east + 8 N west as 18 N instead of 2 N east. They treat forces as scalars because they are used to adding numbers in mathematics without direction.

options.text: Believe "balanced forces mean the object is stationary" because they conflate zero net force with zero velocity.
options.outcome: For example, they see a book on a table (balanced, at rest) and a cricket ball rolling on grass slowing down (unbalanced, friction), but never observe an object with balanced forces in motion because friction is ubiquitous.

c9_physics_ch04.title: Use it in the wild
c9_physics_ch04.scenario: A 60 kg woman climbs a staircase of 20 steps, each 15 cm high, in 10 seconds. She then walks horizontally along a 30 m long corridor at constant speed in 15 seconds. Compare the work done by her against gravity in the two parts of her motion.
c9_physics_ch04.prompt: You are asked: "Explain why she feels tired during the horizontal walk even though work against gravity is zero" — what do you conclude?

options.text: Climbing: 1800 J against gravity. Horizontal walk: 0 J against gravity.
options.outcome: Fatigue during horizontal walk is due to internal muscular work, not physical work on the body against gravity.

options.text: Holding a heavy object stationary (like a 20 kg suitcase) involves "doing work" because their muscles tire.
options.outcome: They reason: "I'm applying an upward force equal to weight, so work = force × distance, but distance is zero... wait, my arms get tired so energy is used, so work must be non-zero."

options.text: Believe "more pulleys always means less effort" and mechanically count total pulleys (fixed + movable) as VR.
options.outcome: The exact error: they think a system with 2 fixed and 2 movable pulleys has VR = 4, but VR equals the number of rope segments supporting the movable block only.

options.text: Confuse "change in kinetic energy" (deltaKE) with "kinetic energy" (KE).
options.outcome: The exact error: they think the Work-Energy Theorem says W = KE, rather than W = deltaKE. In exams, this leads to calculating KE instead of deltaKE, or concluding that zero work means zero KE.

c9_physics_ch05.title: Use it in the wild
c9_physics_ch05.scenario: A hospital wants to image a fetus at 20 weeks gestation (size ~ 25 cm). They have two transducers: one at 2 MHz, another at 10 MHz. The speed of sound in tissue is 1540 m/s.
c9_physics_ch05.prompt: You are asked: "Justify using wavelength and penetration depth concepts" — what do you conclude?

options.text: Use 2 MHz transducer for whole-body overview (better penetration, λ = 0.77 mm). Use 10 MHz transducer for detailed heart imaging (higher resolution, λ = 0.154 mm).

options.outcome: They also think the vibrating object itself "throws" sound particles into the air like projectiles, rather than transferring energy via particle oscillations.

options.text: Think "ultrasound" means "very loud sound" and "infrasound" means "very soft sound," confusing frequency with amplitude.
options.outcome: For example, they might say a loudspeaker playing a low bass note at high volume produces infrasound, not realizing that infrasound is defined solely by frequency (< 20 Hz), not by how loud it is.

options.text: Confuse echo with reverberation.
options.outcome: The exact error: they think any reflected sound is an echo, not distinguishing between a single distinct reflection (echo, far surface) and many overlapping reflections (reverberation, enclosed space).

c9_physics_ch06.title: Use it in the wild
c9_physics_ch06.scenario: A student in Delhi (28.6°N) measures the shadow of a 1.5 m vertical pole at solar noon on the September equinox and finds it to be 0.82 m long. (a) Calculate the solar elevation angle from this measurement. (b) Calculate the solar zenith angle.
c9_physics_ch06.prompt: You are asked: "Explain without calculating" — what do you conclude?

options.text: (a) α ≈ 61.3°, (b) θ ≈ 28.7°, (c) I ≈ 1194 W/m², (d) Lower on December solstice because the Sun is lower in the sky (larger zenith angle) due to the Southward shift of the subsolar point.

options.outcome: atmospheric O₂ would decline over ~100,000 years even if all photosynthesis ceased, because the reservoir is enormous (1.2 × 10¹⁸ kg) relative to annual net imbalance.

options.text: Think that the greenhouse effect is caused by the ozone hole, or that all air pollution (like smog/particulate matter) warms the planet.
options.outcome: the ozone hole is a separate issue (stratospheric ozone depletion by CFCs), and while some aerosols (black carbon) warm, many (sulfates) cool by reflecting sunlight.

c11_chem_ch01.title: Use it in the wild
c11_chem_ch01.scenario: The Bhopal gas tragedy (1984) released methyl isocyanate (MIC). The disaster arose from water ingress into MIC storage tank.
c11_chem_ch01.prompt: You are asked: "Using chemical principles, explain: (a) the reaction of MIC with water, (b) why the reaction is violently exothermic, (c) how green chemistry principles (inherently safer design) could have prevented it" — what do you conclude?

options.text: (a) CH₃NCO + H₂O → CH₃NH₂ + CO₂ (via unstable carbamic acid). (b) High-energy cumulene bonds (N=C=O) hydrolyse to stable products + gas evolution → thermal runaway.
options.outcome: (c) ISD: avoid MIC storage via in situ generation; substitute with less hazardous isocyanates; moderate conditions (dilution, refrigeration, inert blanketing).

options.text: Believe chemistry's relevance is limited to laboratory reactions and textbook equations, failing to recognise that every material object they touch — the polymer in their phone casing (polycarbonate synthesis via phosgene-free route), the nitrogen in their DNA (ultimately from Haber-Bosch ammonia), the fluoride in their toothpaste (SnF₂ remineralisation) — exists because chemists designed molecular pathways to make it.
options.outcome: They confuse "chemical" (adjective, often pejorative) with "chemistry" (science of molecular design).

options.text: Believe the Law of Conservation of Mass means "the mass of solid reactants equals mass of solid products" — they ignore gaseous products or reactants.
options.outcome: if gas leaks, it's not isolated). The precise error: not defining the system boundary to include ALL phases.

options.text: Think the Law of Multiple Proportions applies to the mass ratios within a single compound (e.

c11_chem_ch02.title: Use it in the wild
c11_chem_ch02.scenario: A student sets up a cathode ray tube with a magnetic field perpendicular to the electron beam. The beam deflects in a circular path of radius 5 cm. If the magnetic field is doubled while keeping the accelerating voltage same, what happens to the radius?
c11_chem_ch02.prompt: You are asked: "Justify using the formula for radius of curvature" — what do you conclude?

options.text: Radius becomes 2.5 cm. Because r = mv/(eB) and v is fixed by accelerating voltage, radius is inversely proportional to magnetic field strength.
options.outcome: This choice applies the concept to the real situation before acting.

options.text: Think cathode rays are electromagnetic waves (like light) because they travel in straight lines and cause fluorescence.
options.outcome: They confuse the wave-like properties (straight-line travel, shadow formation) with particle nature.

options.text: Believe the magnetic force on the electron beam is always perpendicular to the velocity, so it cannot change the speed — which is true — but they then incorrectly conclude that the magnetic field does no work and therefore cannot be used to measure e/m.
options.outcome: They forget that the radius of curvature r = mv/(eB) directly contains the ratio e/m, and that measuring r at known v (from the electric-field balance) gives e/m without the magnetic field doing work.

options.text: Believe Rutherford's model "solved" the atomic structure problem and that electrons orbit like planets in stable paths.
options.outcome: The specific error: they ignore that Maxwell's electromagnetic theory (1860s) predicts any accelerating charge (including an electron in circular motion) must radiate energy continuously.

c11_chem_ch03.title: Use it in the wild
c11_chem_ch03.scenario: A newly discovered element X has atomic weight 180. It forms a volatile chloride XCl₄ and an oxide XO₂. In Mendeleev's table, the two neighbouring elements in the same group are A (atomic weight 178, forms ACl₄, AO₂) and B (atomic weight 182, forms BCl₃, B₂O₃).
c11_chem_ch03.prompt: You are asked: "Determine the correct position of X in Mendeleev's table (group and approximate period) and justify your placement using chemical reasoning" — what do you conclude?

options.text: X is placed in Group IV (valency 4), 6th period, alongside A (atomic weight 178). The decision is based on matching valency (from XCl₄ and XO₂) with A, not on atomic weight proximity to B.
options.outcome: This choice applies the concept to the real situation before acting.

options.text: Believe Mendeleev strictly followed increasing atomic weight order.
options.outcome: he deliberately inverted several pairs (Te/I, Ar/K, Co/Ni, Th/Pa) because their chemical properties demanded a different group placement.

options.text: Think the modern periodic table is arranged strictly by increasing atomic mass, confusing it with Mendeleev's table.
options.outcome: They also mistakenly believe that the group number equals the number of valence electrons for all elements (including transition metals), not realizing that for d-block, group number = (n-1)d electrons + ns electrons.

options.text: "The group number equals the number of valence electrons for all elements."
options.outcome: Specific error: Students apply the p-block rule (Group = 10 + valence electrons) or s-block rule (Group = valence electrons) to d-block elements.

c11_chem_ch04.title: Use it in the wild
c11_chem_ch04.scenario: The Lewis structure of ozone (O₃) is often written with one double bond and one single bond. A student argues: "Since all oxygen atoms are identical, the bonds should be identical — so ozone should have 1.5 bonds each, meaning we should draw one and a half lines."
c11_chem_ch04.prompt: You are asked: "Explain why this reasoning is chemically incorrect, and describe what the correct representation (resonance hybrid) actually means for bond length and bond order" — what do you conclude?

options.text: Lewis structures use whole bonds only. Resonance hybrid means the molecule exists as ONE structure where both O–O bonds are equivalent with bond order 1.5 and length ~128 pm.
options.outcome: The "1.5 lines" idea confuses the MODEL (discrete canonical forms) with the REALITY (delocalised electron density).

options.text: Treat the octet rule as absolute: they force octets on all atoms even when impossible (e.
options.outcome: g., drawing 5 bonds on nitrogen in NO₃⁻ to "complete" octet) or refuse expanded octets for period 3+ elements (e.

options.text: Think the octet rule alone drives ionic bond formation: "Atoms transfer electrons to complete octets, so ionic bonds form."
options.outcome: They miss that octet completion in gaseous ions is not enough — the lattice enthalpy must compensate for the net endothermic ion formation.

options.text: Think the central atom is always the one with the lowest electronegativity, but they forget that hydrogen is never a central atom (it can form only one bond).
options.outcome: Another specific error: when drawing Lewis structures for ions like NH4+, they add the positive charge as an extra electron instead of removing one, leading to an incorrect electron count.

c11_chem_ch05.title: Use it in the wild

options.text: Treat "van der Waals forces" as synonymous with "London dispersion forces" only, ignoring dipole-dipole and dipole-induced dipole components.
options.outcome: For example, they explain NH₃'s boiling point (-33°C) solely by London forces, missing its significant dipole-dipole contribution (μ=1.47 D).

options.text: Believe London forces exist ONLY in nonpolar molecules and dipole-dipole forces exist ONLY in polar molecules, treating them as mutually exclusive categories.
options.outcome: ALL molecules (polar and nonpolar) experience London forces; polar molecules experience BOTH London and dipole-dipole forces simultaneously.

options.outcome: They write HCl, H₂S, CH₃Cl as H-bonded.

c11_chem_ch06.title: Use it in the wild
c11_chem_ch06.scenario: A student claims: "In a bomb calorimeter, the reaction occurs in an isolated system, so ΔU = 0 for the combustion reaction." Is the student correct?

options.text: The student is incorrect. The bomb (reaction vessel) is a closed system — it exchanges heat with the surrounding water bath.
options.outcome: The bomb + water bath together form an isolated system (ΔUtotal = 0).

options.text: Think a closed system cannot exchange heat — they equate "closed" with "thermally insulated".
options.outcome: it is closed (matter fixed) but not isolated because heat crosses the boundary. This error propagates to first law problems: they set q = 0 for closed systems, leading to wrong ΔU signs.

options.text: Write the First Law as ΔU = q - w (with w = work done BY system) and use w = +PΔV for expansion work.

options.text: Treat ΔH = ΔU + ΔngRT as universally valid without checking: (1) all species are ideal gases, (2) temperature is constant, (3) Δng counts ONLY gaseous stoichiometric coefficients.
options.outcome: Example error: For 2H₂(g) + O₂(g) → 2H₂O(l), they calculate Δng = 2 – 3 = –1 (wrongly including liquid water as gas) instead of Δng = 0 – 3 = –3.

c11_chem_ch07.title: Use it in the wild

c12_chem_ch02.title: Use it in the wild

options.text: Write the Nernst equation for a full cell as Ecell = E°cell - (0.059/n) log([products]/[reactants]) but incorrectly identify n as the number of electrons in only ONE half-reaction instead of the balanced full cell reaction.

c12_chem_ch03.title: Use it in the wild
c12_chem_ch03.scenario: A student writes the rate of reaction for 3H₂(g) + N₂(g) → 2NH₃(g) as: Rate = –Δ[H₂]/Δt = –Δ[N₂]/Δt = Δ[NH₃]/Δt.

options.text: The student's expression is incorrect. Correct: Rate = –(1/3)Δ[H₂]/Δt = –Δ[N₂]/Δt = (1/2)Δ[NH₃]/Δt.

options.text: Think the rate of reaction equals the rate of change of concentration of any species (Δ[species]/Δt) without the stoichiometric coefficient factor.
options.outcome: For example, in 2N₂O₅ → 4NO₂ + O₂, they write rate = –Δ[N₂O₅]/Δt = Δ[NO₂]/Δt = Δ[O₂]/Δt, which gives three different numbers.

options.text: Write the rate law directly from the balanced equation, e.

options.text: Write the zero-order rate law as Rate = k[R] instead of Rate = k, and then use the first-order integrated equation ln[R] = –kt + ln[R]₀.

c12_chem_ch04.title: Use it in the wild
c12_chem_ch04.scenario: In the modern periodic table, the d-block occupies Groups 3–12. A student argues: "Since Group 12 elements (Zn, Cd, Hg) have completely filled d subshells, they should be moved to the p-block." Evaluate this argument using the IUPAC definition of transition elements, the concept of block classification, and the electronic configuration of Zn.
c12_chem_ch04.prompt: What would be the consequence for the periodic table structure if Group 12 were moved?

options.text: The argument is flawed. Block position is determined by the subshell being filled (3d for Period 4), not by whether the filled subshell is incomplete in ions.
options.outcome: Zn is the 10th element of 3d filling → d-block.

options.text: "All d-block elements are transition elements, and all transition elements have variable oxidation states."
options.outcome: Why it's wrong: (1) Zn, Cd, Hg (Group 12) are d-block but not transition elements because they have d¹⁰ configuration in both atomic and common ionic states (Zn²⁺: 3d¹⁰).

c12_chem_ch10.title: Use it in the wild

options.outcome: This choice applies the concept to the real situation before acting.

options.outcome: They also equate "sugar" with sweetness, but classification is based on hydrolysis, not taste.

options.text: Write the open-chain Fischer projection as the “only” structure of glucose and then try to explain all reactions from it.
options.outcome: They forget that in aqueous solution the cyclic hemiacetals predominate, and they mistakenly think the two anomers are enantiomers (mirror images) rather than diastereomers.

options.text: Routinely write the cyclic structure of fructose as a six-membered pyranose ring (like glucose) because they memorise "monosaccharides form pyranose rings" without counting atoms.
options.outcome: The correct furanose ring has 5 atoms (C-2, C-3, C-4, C-5, O), not 6.

c7_chem_ch01.title: Use it in the wild
c7_chem_ch01.scenario: Two mystery rods (Rod A and Rod B) are tested. Rod A can be drawn into fine wires 0.1 mm thick. Rod B shatters into pieces when hit with a hammer or pulled.
c7_chem_ch01.prompt: Which rod represents a metal, and what distinct properties are being demonstrated?

options.text: Rod A represents a metal because it is ductile (can be drawn into wire), whereas Rod B is a non-metal exhibiting brittleness.
options.outcome: This choice applies the concept to the real situation before acting.

options.text: Assume that all shiny materials are metals and all dull materials are non-metals.
options.outcome: For example, they may classify iodine crystals or graphite (a form of carbon) as metals because they possess a shiny, lustrous appearance, or they may classify pure gold that has lost its polish as a non-metal.

options.text: Confuse "hardness" with "malleability," assuming that any hard object can be beaten into a sheet.
options.outcome: For example, diamond is the hardest natural substance known, yet it is extremely brittle and will shatter if struck with a hammer, whereas a relatively softer metal like gold or lead is highly malleable and can be easily beaten into thin sheets.

options.text: Confuse ductility with malleability, assuming that any material that can be hammered into a sheet can also be automatically drawn into a wire of equal utility, or vice versa.
options.outcome: For example, zinc can be beaten into sheets at certain temperatures but is much less ductile than copper, leading students to mistakenly treat these two mechanical properties as identical.

c7_chem_ch02.title: Use it in the wild
c7_chem_ch02.scenario: Photosynthesis in green plants follows the equation: 6CO2 + 6H2O {Sunlight} C6H12O6 + 6O2.
c7_chem_ch02.prompt: You are asked: "Why is this complex chemical change classified as one of the most vital desirable changes on Earth? Support your answer with biological and chemical reasoning" — what do you conclude?

options.text: Photosynthesis is a highly desirable chemical change because it converts simple inorganic molecules (CO2 and H2O) into energy-rich glucose (C6H12O6) and life-supporting oxygen gas (O2) using solar energy.
options.outcome: This choice applies the concept to the real situation before acting.

options.text: Assume that any change involving a drastic change in appearance, size, or state (such as tearing paper into tiny shreds, boiling water into steam, or dissolving salt in water) is a chemical change because "the original object is gone and cannot be easily put back together."
options.outcome: They confuse physical alterations in dimensions or phase with chemical reactions that rearrange atoms into entirely different molecules.

options.text: Confuse any change that alters appearance, size, or shape (such as tearing paper, cutting vegetables, or breaking chalk) with a chemical change because the original object cannot be glued or put back together easily.
options.outcome: They assume that if an object is permanently altered in form, a new substance must have been created.

options.text: Think that any visible change—such as a change in size, shape, or state (like melting ice or boiling water)—must be a chemical change because something "looks different."
options.outcome: For example, they might believe that melting wax or boiling water creates a new substance because the liquid water is no longer visible as ice or steam.

c8_chem_ch02.title: Use it in the wild
c8_chem_ch02.scenario: Two drops of ink are added simultaneously to two separate beakers: one containing ice-cold water at 5°C and the other containing hot water at 70°C. Without stirring, the ink in the hot water spreads out much faster. Connect this observation to the particulate nature of matter and thermal energy.
c8_chem_ch02.prompt: What is the best explanation or next step?

options.text: In hot water, water particles possess higher kinetic energy and move much faster than in cold water. This rapid movement causes faster collisions with the ink particles, leading to quicker spreading (diffusion) of the ink throughout the beaker.
options.outcome: This choice applies the concept to the real situation before acting.

options.text: Think that when a solid dissolves in a liquid (like salt in water), the solid matter vanishes or turns completely into liquid, rather than breaking down into microscopic particles that disperse among the liquid particles.
options.outcome: Students often think that when a solid dissolves in a liquid (like salt in water), the solid matter vanishes or turns completely into liquid, rather than breaking down into microscopic particles that disperse among the liquid particles.

c8_chem_ch03.title: Use it in the wild
c8_chem_ch03.scenario: Two identical sealed glass bulbs, Bulb A and Bulb B, contain gases at standard temperature and pressure. Bulb A contains pure oxygen gas (O2), while Bulb B contains clean atmospheric air. If an identical burning candle is placed into each bulb after breaking the seals, predict which candle will burn longer and provide full chemical reasoning based on composition.
c8_chem_ch03.prompt: What is the best explanation or next step?

options.text: The candle in Bulb A (pure oxygen) will burn much more intensely and longer than the one in Bulb B (atmospheric air) because Bulb A has a 100% oxygen concentration compared to only 21% in air, providing a much higher supply of the reactant required for combustion.
options.outcome: This choice applies the concept to the real situation before acting.

options.text: Think that when a solid dissolves in a liquid (like sugar in water), a chemical reaction has occurred to form a new substance because the solid "disappears."
options.outcome: They fail to realize that dissolving is a physical mixing process where the solute particles merely disperse among the solvent molecules, and the original substance can be recovered intact by evaporation.

options.text: Assume that because a mixture is uniform and clear (like a sugar solution or salt solution), a chemical reaction must have occurred to form a new compound.
options.outcome: For example, when making sugar syrup (Chashni) for Indian sweets, they believe that since the white sugar crystals "disappear" into the water and cannot be filtered out with a tea strainer, a new chemical compound has been formed.

options.text: Believe that alloys are pure substances or chemical compounds because they look uniform (homogeneous) and have fixed commercial names like "brass" or "steel."
options.outcome: They fail to realize that unlike water (H2O) or sodium chloride (NaCl), alloys do not have a fixed chemical formula and their composition can vary within certain percentage ranges.

c9_chem_ch01.title: Use it in the wild
c9_chem_ch01.scenario: In a pharmaceutical quality control lab, you must verify that a batch of paracetamol syrup is a true solution (homogeneous) and not a colloidal suspension (heterogeneous). The syrup is viscous and slightly yellow.
c9_chem_ch01.prompt: You are asked: "Propose a three-step experimental protocol using only: centrifuge, filter paper (0.2 µm pore), and laser pointer" — what do you conclude?

options.text: Protocol: 1) Tyndall test with laser: true solution = no beam; colloid = visible beam. 2) Filtration (0.2 µm): both pass completely (not discriminatory).
options.outcome: 3) Centrifugation (10,000 rpm, 30 min): true solution = no pellet; colloid = visible pellet.

options.text: Think "homogeneous means you can't see particles with naked eye" and classify colloids like milk or starch solution as homogeneous because they appear uniform.
options.outcome: The exact error: they ignore that colloids have particle size 1-1000 nm (larger than true solutions <1 nm), show Tyndall effect, and are microscopically heterogeneous.

options.text: Think colloids are homogeneous because they look uniform and transparent (like milk or jelly).
options.outcome: They confuse "appears uniform to the eye" with "homogeneous at the particle level".

options.text: Think the Tyndall effect is caused by the colour of the colloid (e.
options.outcome: g., milk is white, so it scatters light).

c9_chem_ch02.title: Use it in the wild
c9_chem_ch02.scenario: In a mass spectrometer, singly ionized atoms of two isotopes of chlorine (3517 Cl and 3717 Cl) are accelerated through the same voltage and then enter a uniform magnetic field. Which isotope will hit the detector at a larger radius?
c9_chem_ch02.prompt: You are asked: "Justify using the properties of subatomic particles" — what do you conclude?

options.text: 3717 Cl will hit at a larger radius because it has more neutrons, giving it greater mass while charge remains the same; radius is proportional to square root of mass for fixed charge and accelerating voltage.
options.outcome: This choice applies the concept to the real situation before acting.

options.text: Believe that because electrons orbit the nucleus, they must have significant mass like planets orbiting the sun.
options.outcome: electron mass is 1/1837 u – it contributes almost nothing to atomic mass. This error stems from visualizing the atom as a solar system rather than a quantum entity.

options.text: Think Bohr's model "failed" because electrons don't actually move in circular orbits like planets.
options.outcome: move in circular orbits like planets.

options.text: Think Thomson's model has electrons orbiting in the positive sphere, like a mini solar system.
options.outcome: They draw electrons on circular paths. This is wrong: Thomson explicitly proposed electrons are stationary (or oscillating slightly) at fixed positions in the sphere — the "plums" don't move.

c9_chem_ch03.title: Use it in the wild
c9_chem_ch03.scenario: A teacher sets up two experiments: (1) 2 g hydrogen + 16 g oxygen → water in a sealed steel bomb. (2) 2 g hydrogen + 16 g oxygen → water in an open beaker with a spark. In both, the reactants are exactly the same masses.
c9_chem_ch03.prompt: You are asked: "Use the term "system boundary" in your answer" — what do you conclude?

options.text: The sealed bomb is a closed system — its rigid walls prevent any mass exchange, so 18 g reactants yield 18 g products inside. The open beaker is an open system — water vapour escapes into the air, so the beaker+liquid mass decreases.
options.outcome: The law holds for the universe, but not for an arbitrarily chosen open container.

options.text: Believe the Law of Conservation of Mass means "mass never changes in ANY reaction," so when they see magnesium ribbon burn in an open crucible and the mass increases (Mg + ½O₂ → MgO), they think the law is broken.
options.outcome: The exact error: they confuse the SYSTEM (magnesium only) with the REACTION (magnesium + oxygen). They weigh only the solid before and after, ignoring that oxygen from air entered the system.

options.text: Treat the subscript outside parentheses in polyatomic ions as applying only to the first atom inside.
options.outcome: Example: In Ca₃(PO₄)₂, they calculate P as 1 atom and O as 4 atoms (instead of P=2, O=8). They write: 3×Ca + 1×P + 4×O.

options.text: Believe the Law of Constant Proportions applies to the total mass of reactants and products (e.
options.outcome: g., "2g hydrogen + 16g oxygen → 18g water, so the law means total mass is fixed").

c6_chemistry_ch04.title: Use it in the wild
c6_chemistry_ch04.scenario: If you were tasked with making a statue that must last for 500 years in a rainy city, would you choose iron or gold?
c6_chemistry_ch04.prompt: You are asked: "Explain your reasoning using the concept of reactivity" — what do you conclude?

options.text: Gold, because it is inert and will not react with the rainwater or air, ensuring the statue maintains its original form, whereas iron would rust away.
options.outcome: This choice applies the concept to the real situation before acting.

options.text: Confuse "transparent" with "colorless."
options.outcome: They might think a colored glass is opaque because it isn't perfectly clear.

options.text: Think that if a material is hard, it must be metal, or if it is soft, it cannot be a metal.
options.outcome: For example, they might think a sponge is not a "real" material because it is soft, or that all metals must be extremely hard.

options.text: Believe that "rust" is just a layer of dirt that can be washed off.
options.outcome: the iron has been converted into iron oxide, meaning the metal is being destroyed and weakened.

c6_chemistry_ch05.title: Use it in the wild
c6_chemistry_ch05.scenario: If you observe a metal fence, what evidence would suggest it is undergoing a slow change?
c6_chemistry_ch05.prompt: What is the best explanation or next step?

options.text: A change in color to a brownish-red indicates rust, which is evidence of a slow chemical change occurring over time.
options.outcome: This choice applies the concept to the real situation before acting.

options.text: Believe that if a change is "permanent" or "drastic" (like breaking an object), it cannot be physical.
options.outcome: They mistakenly assume that physical changes must be easily "reversible," like melting ice.

options.text: Believe that any change in appearance (like color) or any change involving heat is a chemical change.
options.outcome: They fail to realize that ice melting or water boiling (which involves heat) are physical changes because the substance remains the same.

options.text: Believe that rusting is just "dirt" or "stains" that can be wiped off, or that it is a physical change like melting ice.
options.outcome: This happens because they confuse the surface layer of rust with an external coating rather than recognizing it as a transformed portion of the metal itself.

c11_bio_ch01.title: Use it in the wild
c11_bio_ch01.scenario: In the Western Ghats, a rare orchid species (Species X) reproduces exclusively by vegetative propagation (asexual) through rhizome fragmentation. A closely related species (Species Y) reproduces sexually via insect pollination. Climate models predict 3°C warming and altered rainfall patterns over 50 years.
c11_bio_ch01.prompt: You are asked: "Predict which species has higher extinction risk and justify using metabolic, reproductive, and evolutionary principles" — what do you conclude?

options.text: Species X (asexual orchid) has higher extinction risk. Zero genetic variation prevents evolutionary adaptation to 3°C warming.
options.outcome: Its fixed metabolic phenotype cannot adjust to new temperature/rainfall regimes.

options.text: Equate "movement" with life (e.
options.outcome: g., "fire moves, so it's alive") or "growth" with any size increase (crystal, raisin).

options.text: Believe "growth = increase in size/weight" and equate it with non-living accretion (crystal, snowball).
options.outcome: The exact wrong reasoning: "Since both a growing child and a growing crystal become larger and heavier, growth cannot distinguish living from non-living."

options.text: Equate "cellular organisation" with merely "being made of cells" — they miss that it specifically means HIERARCHICAL organisation (cell→tissue→organ→system) with DIVISION OF LABOUR.
options.outcome: They also believe consciousness REQUIRES a brain/nervous system, so they classify plants as "non-conscious."

c11_bio_ch02.title: Use it in the wild
c11_bio_ch02.scenario: A water sample from a hot spring (75°C, pH 2) yields a prokaryote that oxidizes elemental sulfur to sulfuric acid for energy and fixes CO₂. It has no peptidoglycan in its wall.
c11_bio_ch02.prompt: You are asked: "Classify this organism at the sub-kingdom level, name its nutritional category, and explain why it cannot be cultured on standard nutrient agar plates" — what do you conclude?

options.text: Sub-kingdom: Archaebacteria (thermoacidophile). Nutrition: Chemosynthetic autotroph.
options.outcome: Cannot grow on nutrient agar because it requires 75°C, pH 2, inorganic sulfur energy source, and CO₂ carbon source — conditions opposite to standard lab media.

options.text: Believe Whittaker's system is the "final, correct" classification and that Kingdom Protista is a natural, monophyletic group.
options.outcome: They fail to recognize that the exam explicitly states Protista's boundaries are "not well defined" and that the three-domain system (Archaea, Bacteria, Eukarya) was proposed later because Monera contained two phylogenetically distinct prokaryotic lineages (Archaebacteria vs Eubacteria).

options.text: Think "blue-green algae" (cyanobacteria) are algae (eukaryotic protists) because they are photosynthetic, filamentous, and form blooms in water.
options.outcome: They forget that cyanobacteria lack a nucleus, have prokaryotic ribosomes (70S), thylakoids not enclosed in chloroplasts, and a peptidoglycan wall — all placing them firmly in Monera.

options.text: Believe endospore formation is a form of reproduction because "a new structure forms from the cell."
options.outcome: The error is conflating survival structures with reproductive output.

c11_bio_ch03.title: Use it in the wild
c11_bio_ch03.scenario: A researcher claims to have discovered a "missing link" plant fossil from the Devonian period showing: (1) well-developed xylem and phloem, (2) heterospory (microspores and megaspores), (3) megaspores retained in megasporangia on the parent sporophyte, (4) microspores developing into pollen-like structures, but (5) no integument surrounding the megasporangium (i.e., no true ovule).
c11_bio_ch03.prompt: Based on your understanding of plant evolution and classification, which major group does this fossil most likely represent, and why is it significant for understanding the origin of Phanerogamae?

options.text: The fossil represents a transitional form between heterosporous pteridophytes and gymnosperms (progymnosperm/seed fern). It is significant because it demonstrates the stepwise evolution of the seed habit: heterospory → megaspore retention → pollen → integument.
options.outcome: This confirms Phanerogamae evolved from within Cryptogamae (pteridophytes), making Cryptogamae paraphyletic.

options.text: Think "Cryptogamae = lower plants without vascular tissue" and "Phanerogamae = higher plants with vascular tissue."
options.outcome: This is wrong because pteridophytes (ferns, Selaginella) are Cryptogamae but possess well-developed xylem and phloem, true roots, stems, and leaves.

options.text: Believe "all algae have flagellated zoospores and gametes" because textbook examples (Chlamydomonas, Ulothrix, Volvox) are flagellated.
options.outcome: They miss that Rhodophyceae completely lack flagella in both asexual (non-motile spores) and sexual (non-motile spermatia) reproduction, and that Phaeophyceae zoospores have two unequal lateral flagella (not equal/apical like Chlorophyceae).

options.text: Believe "brown algae are brown because they lack chlorophyll" and "red algae are red because they lack chlorophyll."
options.outcome: ALL three classes possess chlorophyll a; the colour differences arise from accessory pigments (fucoxanthin, phycoerythrin) masking chlorophyll's green.

c11_bio_ch04.title: Use it in the wild
c11_bio_ch04.scenario: In the Andaman reefs, a coral (Anthozoa) colony suffers bleaching after a thermal spike. The symbiotic zooxanthellae are expelled, leaving the coral transparent.
c11_bio_ch04.prompt: You are asked: "Predict the cascading effects on the coral's nutrition, calcification, and colony survival over 30 days, linking each effect to the loss of photosynthetic products" — what do you conclude?

options.text: Bleaching causes: (1) Severe energy deficit as 90% photosynthate supply lost; heterotrophy cannot compensate. (2) Calcification stops due to loss of ATP and pH regulation from photosynthesis.
options.outcome: (3) Colony dies via tissue catabolism and algal overgrowth within 30 days unless symbionts return.

options.text: Believe "radial symmetry = diploblastic" and "bilateral symmetry = triploblastic = coelomate" as rigid one-to-one mappings.
options.outcome: Specifically, they fail to recognise that Echinodermata are triploblastic coelomates with secondary radial symmetry (adults), and that Platyhelminthes are triploblastic bilaterians without a coelom (acoelomates).

options.text: Believe "organ level of organisation" and "organ system level of organisation" differ only in the number of organs present, and that Platyhelminthes have organ systems because they possess multiple organs (brain, eyespots, flame cells, gonads).
options.outcome: The exact error: they miss that organ-system level requires FUNCTIONAL INTEGRATION of organs into physiological systems (e.

options.text: Think sponges are "diploblastic" because they see two cell layers (pinacoderm outside, choanoderm inside).
options.outcome: They confuse differentiated cell layers with embryonic germ layers.

c11_bio_ch05.title: Use it in the wild
c11_bio_ch05.scenario: In a coastal reclamation project, you must choose between planting Casuarina (she-oak) and Avicennia (mangrove) for stabilising newly deposited tidal mudflats. Compare their root adaptations for (a) anchorage in fluid sediment, (b) oxygen supply to roots, and (c) salt tolerance mechanism.
c11_bio_ch05.prompt: Which genus would you select for the first 5 years and why?

options.text: Select Avicennia for first 5 years. Its pneumatophores ensure root respiration in anaerobic mud, cable roots bind surface sediment, and salt secretion/exclusion mechanisms allow survival in high salinity — Casuarina lacks these specific adaptations.
options.outcome: This choice applies the concept to the real situation before acting.

options.text: Believe "all underground parts are roots" and therefore classify potato tubers, ginger rhizomes, and onion bulbs as root modifications because they grow below ground and store food.
options.outcome: The exact error: they ignore the morphological criteria — nodes, internodes, scale leaves, and axillary buds — that define stems, and they fail to apply the developmental-origin test (radicle vs. plumule).

options.text: Think "underground stem = root" because both are below soil and store food.
options.outcome: They specifically argue: "Potato is a root because it's underground and swollen with starch."

options.text: Confuse phyllotaxy (arrangement of leaves on stem) with venation (arrangement of veins in lamina), often describing a leaf as "alternate venation" or "reticulate phyllotaxy."
options.outcome: This stems from treating both as "patterns" without recognizing they operate at different hierarchical levels: phyllotaxy is a shoot-system trait (node-level), venation is a leaf-organ trait (lamina-level).

c11_bio_ch06.title: Use it in the wild
c11_bio_ch06.scenario: A student examines a transverse section of an unknown plant stem and records: (1) Vascular bundles are scattered in the ground tissue. (2) Each bundle is surrounded by a distinct sclerenchymatous bundle sheath. (3) Phloem parenchyma is absent.
c11_bio_ch06.prompt: You are asked: "Justify each feature with the anatomical principle it represents" — what do you conclude?

options.text: Monocot stem. Justification: Scattered bundles + sclerenchymatous bundle sheath + absent phloem parenchyma + Y-shaped xylem are collectively diagnostic of monocot stem anatomy (e.
options.outcome: g.

options.text: Meristematic tissue exists only at the root and shoot tips (apical meristem) and are unaware of lateral meristem (vascular cambium, cork cambium) responsible for secondary growth in dicots, or intercalary meristem at grass nodes that enables regrowth after grazing.
options.outcome: This leads to an inability to explain how a mango trunk thickens over years or why lawn grass recovers quickly after mowing.

options.text: Believe "collenchyma and sclerenchyma are both mechanical tissues, so they are interchangeable."
options.outcome: They fail to grasp that collenchyma's living, plastically extensible primary walls allow organ elongation (e.

options.text: Believe phloem transports water and minerals along with food because "sap" is a liquid.
